title: ‘I’m Not MAGA,’ Says Man in MAGA Hat
excerpt: Elon Musk doesn’t know where people got the idea that he’s MAGA. “I’m not MAGA,” he said in an interview yesterday. “I’m not sure what MAGA means.” He went on t
body: Elon Musk doesn’t know where people got the idea that he’s MAGA. “I’m not MAGA,” he said in an interview yesterday. “I’m not sure what MAGA means.” He went on to describe himself as “ideologically quite moderate” and added, “I don’t think I have, like, any kind of extreme political views.” This is the same Elon Musk who last year took the stage at the Conservative Political Action Conference wearing a black MAGA hat and wielding a chainsaw, has opined that “whites are a rapidly dying minority,” called the left “the party of murder,” posted that he loves Donald Trump “as much as a straight man can love another man,” spearheaded the Trump administration’s DOGE initiative, was the largest individual donor to Republicans in the past two elections, and just two weeks ago urged his 240 million–plus followers to “Vote red today!” on the social-media platform that he bought to wage war on the “woke mind virus.” The world’s richest man, it seems, has changed his tune

The nearly half a billion dollars that he spent supporting Republican candidates in the 2026 midterms? That was aimed only at ensuring “checks and balances” in government, he said onstage at The New York Times ’ DealBook Summit yesterday
After the historic Democratic landslide, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO is trying to do what corporate executives often do: adjust their politics to align with the party in power
Mark Zuckerberg banned Trump from Facebook after the Capitol riot on January 6, 2021; four years later, he was standing alongside Trump on the inauguration dais

Palantir CEO Alex Karp donated $1 million to a pro-Trump PAC in December 2024; last week, he told Politico that he’s a lifelong Democrat and that Palantir’s products are “essentially progressive.” Musk’s conversion might be the least convincing yet

It’s tricky enough for a chameleon like Zuckerberg to mold his politics to the moment; most Republicans didn’t buy him as a dripped-out, flag-waving, mixed-martial-arts fan any more than most Democrats bought Facebook’s “pivot to privacy” in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica data-harvesting scandal
Musk pitching the public on his new persona as a buttoned-down centrist is like Senator Elizabeth Warren starring in a Cybertruck commercial
He has said in the past that he voted for Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Joe Biden

His public swerve to the right began during the coronavirus pandemic and fed on his growing resentments about lockdown policies, transgender rights, and the Biden administration’s exclusion of Tesla from a White House event promoting electric vehicles
He moved from California to Texas in 2020, complaining about regulatory burdens, and brought his companies with him

After going all-in on the GOP, Musk now figures to be among the top targets for investigation by a Democrat-led Congress. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts posted on Election Day
And Musk’s business empire is in the awkward position of relying on government contracts and regulatory approvals that will be controlled by political leaders whose party and values he has demonized

Nowhere is this problem more acute for Musk than in his adopted home state of Texas, where the Democrats Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico defeated the Republicans he had backed for governor and the Senate, respectively
Both had campaigned against Musk and data centers. (Musk did not respond to a request for comment.) In the past, Musk has criticized politicians who publicly challenged him

When Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon called for a billionaire tax in 2021, he replied with typical delicacy: “Why does ur pp look like u just came?” Since the midterms, however, Musk has exercised uncharacteristic restraint, especially with Hinojosa, who will soon have leverage over not only data centers but also a major planned expansion of SpaceX’s Starbase, Musk’s massive Terafab semiconductor project, and the appointment of judges to the state’s business courts

Two days after the election, he shared a post characterizing Hinojosa’s approach to data centers as “reasonable” and praising her as “a political talent.” That same week, Hinojosa requested a pause on the state’s consideration of a major land sale to SpaceX until she takes office, in January. “We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms,” she said in a CNN interview

Yesterday, Musk reiterated his openness to working with Hinojosa, whom he called by her first name. “Based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor,” he said
Mockable as Musk’s pivot might be, there’s a strategic logic to it that doesn’t depend on anyone actually believing that he’s sincere
He made the comments at a conference aimed at business insiders, investors, and policy makers
Tesla and SpaceX stocks took a hit from the midterm results, and Musk has a long history of temporarily pulling back from partisanship when he feels that his business interests are vulnerable
Investors probably don’t care as much about Musk’s politics as they care whether he remains capable of making that trade-off when needed
Musk has floated merging SpaceX and Tesla into one conglomerate, which would require approval from shareholders
And then there are the Democratic politicians Musk hopes to appease at least enough to keep his federal contacts and push through key business deals
Here, too, he doesn’t need them to believe in his conversion
He just needs to signal that he’s open to finding some common ground
Many politicians, after all, recognize the value of malleability in service of expediency

Musk’s moderation might well prove short-lived if Democrats don’t respond the way he hopes. (After Musk’s comments yesterday, Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona posted on X: “You are still getting a subpoena.”) Regardless, his sudden circumspection suggests that something significant has already shifted: People watch their words only when they fear consequences
For two years, staying on Trump’s good side was a guarantee of protection for Musk, freeing him to say and do whatever else he wanted

title: The Limits of Positive Thinking
excerpt: A s anxious Americans dealt with a cascade of computer failures over the past week, Donald Trump offered this advice: “Relax.” The air-traffic-control system, e
body: A s anxious Americans dealt with a cascade of computer failures over the past week, Donald Trump offered this advice: “Relax.” The air-traffic-control system, email providers, banks, airlines, and even the internal communications system of the country’s biggest intelligence agency had all seen outages, fueling fears of digital conspiracy
But they weren’t connected, the president assured Fox News
And hackers were not behind the outages, he insisted, because no one would dare risk retaliation by the United States
Companies were simply replacing outdated equipment, “and things happen when you put in new equipment,” he said
There was nothing to see here, no cause for alarm. “Everything’s good.” Digital-security experts are not nearly so sanguine
They see something new and potentially ominous that’s fueling these hugely disruptive outages: artificial intelligence
Companies haven’t been replacing old equipment so much as rapidly patching newly discovered flaws in their systems with the help of sophisticated AI that can quickly spot vulnerabilities
And why are companies moving so fast? Because attackers have AI too
The FBI warned this week about an AI-enabled tool set, called ARTEX, that “cybercriminals and state-aligned hackers” are using to identify weakness and develop attacks in under three hours
None of the affected companies has said that it thinks its systems went down because of an attack
But security experts told us that in the past few weeks, they have been struggling to keep up with an onslaught of attempted hacks from AI-enabled adversaries
And rushing to harden lots of computer infrastructure all at once can be messy and inconsistent, explaining some of the disruptions
Trump has never fully reckoned with the risks of AI
He prefers to call it “superintelligence,” an odd choice given that that’s the term some doomsayers use for AI that becomes self-aware and tries to wipe out humanity
The president frames the race to develop advanced AI as an existential contest between China and the United States. “Whoever wins AI wins,” he is fond of saying
The Defense Department has deployed AI systems across its networks with seemingly little regard for the risks of using them in combat
Trump has avoided creating safety regulations and guardrails and has followed the counsel of executives whose fortunes depend on AI expansion
That includes ex–Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has consistently downplayed the risk of out-of-control AI, calling apocalyptic scenarios “made-up” or baseless
When it comes to developing and deploying the technology, Trump is all gas and no brakes
For a different president, the nerve-racking outages of the past week might have been a moment for sober reflection on whether the United States is prepared for what’s coming

Even some Republicans are asking for that, as are some Democrats. “It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, a Democrat who is in line to chair the Senate Intelligence Committee in the next Congress, said in a statement

Warner has proposed legislation that would subject AI models to greater scrutiny and safety checks. “Americans deserve clear, reliable information and a government that is prepared to respond,” Warner said
But the administration seems not to grasp how worried many Americans are at suddenly being unable to check their bank balance or read their email
The disappearance of everyday conveniences comes after months of dark warnings about rogue AI agents and renewed fears of cyberattacks from Iran
The French government publicly accused Iran last week of remotely sabotaging food-refrigeration units and causing mass spoilage in grocery stores

Trump may insist that there’s nothing to be concerned about, but even some of his allies fear that something bigger is at play. “If this is all a coincidence,” Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, a Republican, told reporters on Tuesday, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” N ormally, in the middle of a domestic crisis, an administration tries to speak with one voice and tell a coherent story to an anxious public
But as bank websites crashed at the same time as stranded passengers slept in airports, no one in the administration seemed to know what was happening or who was in charge of fixing things

On Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who is supposed to lead the government’s response to domestic cybersecurity incidents, suggested that artificial intelligence deployed on computer networks was “self-fixing itself.” In the scenario he described, recent network collapses were the result of a big, messy patching job
That is close to what experts think is continuing to happen

But Mullin attributed his understanding to a tech leader, whom he declined to name, telling Fox News that his theory “kind of makes sense.” This uncertain description, from an official with access to an array of classified government intelligence and seasoned briefers, did little to allay concerns. [ Read: The secretary of imprecision ] The unit within Mullin’s department that should be running point in this crisis, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency , has lost almost a third of its 3,200 employees since Trump returned to office two years ago
The White House wants to cut the budget for some agency programs, including election security, by $700 million next year

When we went to the CISA website today, we found guidance about recent incidents, forms for reporting cyberattacks, and a two-month-old handbook for “Communicating Under Pressure.” “During service outages, clear communication matters,” CISA unironically advised

Officials dismissed any connection between the computer failures and the deep staffing and budget cuts at the agency. “The implication that the recent events would not have occurred if CISA had more employees is patently false,” a White House official said

The new director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, told a congressional committee yesterday that “the timing of these ​incidents can raise questions, ​and it should,” but he insisted that the outages were coincidental and “associated with maintenance and ​technical ​changes.” Clayton also blamed the patching of vulnerabilities, but he didn’t blame AI
Marco Rubio , the secretary of state and the national security adviser, appeared initially confused when a reporter asked at a press conference in Manila whether AI had played a role in the outages
He said he couldn’t confirm that that was the case but explained why AI hypothetically could have led to the systems failing

Rubio stressed that “people are fearful; people are uncertain” and said that it was important for the administration to “share with them transparently what we know.” T rump’s habit, when he is confronted with a crisis, is to rely on the power of positive thinking
In the first weeks of 2020, he was slow to sound the alarm on a new virus discovered in China, reportedly for fear of rattling financial markets and upsetting Xi Jinping
By the time he left office a year later, some 400,000 people in the United States had died of COVID-19
A similar dynamic now seems to be at work

title: Grand Theft Auto VI Is Really Weird
excerpt: J ason Duval lives in a shack on the Leonida Keys, in the simulated Florida where Grand Theft Auto VI is set
body: J ason Duval lives in a shack on the Leonida Keys, in the simulated Florida where Grand Theft Auto VI is set

I began playing the game after its release at midnight, and I have already tried and failed to outrun the police, roamed the hallways of a prison, driven a speedboat to collect cocaine dropped by a seaplane pilot who was skimming from a more upmarket criminal, and flown the seaplane to escape an RV park full of wild-animal-and-narcotics traffickers
If you know anything at all about the game, which almost 5,000 people worked on for more than a decade at a reported cost of more than $1 billion, it is that Leonida is enormous
Early reviewers are bragging on social media about spending more than 100 hours in the world of the game, while only scratching the surface of what is possible

The prospect seems overwhelming because I already have a life that requires labor and demands diversion, and I am worried about how to fit GTA VI ’s simulated work and recreation into my supposedly real life
Theorists of video games (a real thing that I could be accused of being) have a name for this phenomenon: playbor , a portmanteau of play and labor

Many jobs feel fake now anyway—“email jobs,” they were scornfully called even before AI could be mustered to carry out their pointlessness—and games feel like jobs, with a seemingly endless list of menial tasks for their players. [ Read: The least productive day of the year ] An hour or so in, though, the game offers a breather to look around and get your bearings
I decide to stay in Jason’s house instead of venturing out into even a tiny corner of Leonida
There is so much to do here that I find myself wondering how many hours I might spend indoors, inside the pretend home of a fake man
After all, I pass most of my own life as a real man inside my real home, working and puttering, instead of exploring the city or countryside that contain me
J ason has a pet snake, and walking by its glass habitat triggers a text overlay indicating that I can interact with it
I press a button to feed the snake, and Jason reaches into a blue plastic container, carefully retrieves a mouse, and drops it into the cage
I can see another mouse or two in there, of varied shades
I already feel as though I need to resupply the snake food

I find myself wondering where one goes for snake mice, and what that shop might be called in Grand Theft Auto . “Thoughtful actions will increase your focus bar,” the game tells me after I feed the animal
Feeding a snake is thoughtful, apparently
A purple icon animates and a corresponding purple bar fills slightly to communicate the effect of the act
Jason’s stamina and strength are also measured in health-bar form
Some games allocate a bar for hunger or even bladder level
This kind of thing used to seem ridiculous, a perverse way to understand human behavior for the nerds who design and play video games
But when I look at my real smartwatch on my actual wrist, I realize the world has caught up
It translates my movement into a number on a red bar that supposedly represents my activity
I don’t believe that the numbers—383 calories so far today—are real, but I orient my activities around them every day
Better do a quick Peloton to close my rings; time for another walk to get my steps in
I don’t think about it much anymore, but I have become a video-game avatar of myself
I n the shack, morning light pours across a desk from a window whose blinds are raised halfway
On the desk are a radio, a few books, and a conch shell
You know that a video-game object is relevant when it receives an overlay with a text description and an icon of the controller button used to interact with it
In this case, the radio’s channels can be changed with a button on my PlayStation 5 controller, and the book can be examined with a different button
After flipping to a station called Afrobank FM, I examine the book
It’s called Orca: A Whole Different Animal
It’s a send-up of the Navy SEALs and the kind of inspirational title that a former officer might write as CEO of a private mercenary firm or in anticipation of running for a U.S
I can open the book, which contains actual text on simulated pages

I’ve read that Rockstar Games, the creator of GTA , did not use generative AI during the production of the game, and instead employs a large team of people who create all of the media inside it—including Orca , presumably
I wonder whether libraries or bookstores exist in the game, which I might then treat as a laborious literary experience rather than a criminal-underworld fantasy
But flipping through Orca reveals that the game surfaces only a few pages
The book is not real, in the sense that a book contains writing sufficient to justify a book
It is, instead, an icon of a book, like the conch is an icon for decor
I somewhat wish that Rockstar had used AI to generate books instead
I assume—I haven’t looked yet—that someone has, by now, generated a real, fake version of Orca: A Whole Different Animal and put it up for sale on Amazon

title: I Baked My Way Through The Atlantic ’s Archives
excerpt: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
body: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
The most cherished recipes are usually the hardest to follow
They live on stained index cards and notes worn thin at the creases, in handwriting so faded you have to squint to read it
That handwriting belongs to a grandmother or a distant relative, and it was meant for someone who already knew the dish: Add a pinch of this, a teacup of that; bake until done
I’ve spent a lot of time in The Atlantic ’s archives, and I kept running into such recipes tucked into letters, essays, and memoirs, rarely where you’d expect them
I was curious to know whether they still work—and, more important, how they taste
The further back I went, the less my finds looked like recipes
They read like stories, and you had to read closely to find the instructions
Take this “ Letter to a Young Housekeeper ,” from November 1865, written by C
Hawes to “M.,” a bride newly married to “H.” Hawes spends most of the letter arguing that cooking is a fine art and a science, which the woman of the house should learn for herself
She is funny about it, and a little grand

Recalling one early success at the table, Hawes reaches for Henry David Thoreau, whose essays had recently run in this magazine, to describe the dishes: “We ate, lingered, and revelled in them, thus becoming epicures at once … They were as great a revelation to the palate as Bettine or Thoreau might be to the mind.” Only at the very end does she mention a “well-tested” recipe for bread: a quart of milk, a teacup of “hopyeast,” and enough flour “to make it quite stiff.” How much flour? How hot an oven? And how long does it bake for? Hawes doesn’t say
For much of history, recipes moved from one cook to another by word of mouth and by experience: watching a mother at the stove, having a neighbor ask for a missing ingredient
Cookbooks didn’t exist simply because, for centuries, most women couldn’t read, Sarah Lohman, a culinary historian, told me
As literacy spread in the 18th century, women began keeping handwritten notes of family recipes to pass down or to copy for a daughter when she was married
Those recipes were light on instructions by design
They expected you to rely on your instincts “to know when the batter looks right or to know when the cake is done,” Lohman said

By the early 20th century, written recipes had become something to amass, and cookbooks were treated as literature. “It was with something of a shock that I woke one morning and found myself a collector of cookery books,” the American writer Elizabeth Robins Pennell wrote in The Atlantic in 1901
What she prized most were the traces that earlier owners of the books left behind

Her copy of The Queen-Like Closet , a 17th-century cookbook by Hannah Woolley, had several owners before it reached her—one of whom was a young woman named Mary Halfpenny, who had received it as a gift in 1678 and went on to add her own recipes to its pages
A century later, another family used it as their “Bible,” recording their children’s births in the margins
Pennell loved those scribbles: “They add a distinctly personal charm to the shabby little old cookery book.” And sometimes, the actual Bible held recipes too

In 1910, a writer in this magazine’s Contributors’ Club described the family Bible as a place where you might find anything tucked between the pages, from a father’s old report cards “to mother’s recipe for sponge-cake.” But around midcentury, the American recipe changed shape, in part due to technology
I asked Lohman why some of the 19th-century recipes I’d baked didn’t call for butter or eggs

Before the advent of the refrigerator, Lohman explained, these ingredients were seasonal: Cows give milk after calving, from late winter into summer, and hens tend to take a break from laying in winter
Sure enough, the 19th-century recipes missing those ingredients were fall and winter dishes
By the mid-1950s, the majority of American homes had a refrigerator
As kitchens changed, recipes changed with them: more exact, more complete, easier for a stranger to follow
But the story behind the food has never quite gone away
Even as recipes grew more precise and the ingredients in them stopped shifting with the seasons, the people who wrote them kept reaching for memories

In 1985, Corby Kummer, then an editor at The Atlantic , began an essay on pie not with flour or butter but with a tale about his mother’s pie crust, an unforgettable taste that “has driven me to pursue the elusive art of making pastry.” And as recipes moved online, the stories came with them

Food blogs, and later videos, wrapped their instructions in anecdotes; anyone who has looked up a recipe on their phone knows the feeling of scrolling past several paragraphs of backstory before the ingredient list appears
Some of that is less sentimental than it seems (long blocks of text help a recipe rank higher in search results and make more room for ads)
Still, it is telling that when food writers have space to fill, they fill it with stories
I have been baking since I was a child, learning from my mother and grandmothers and from recipes handed down for generations
I was curious whether the recipes I found from over the decades still hold up today
So I baked my way through the archives, beginning with Hawes’s 1865 biscuits and ending on a batch of brownies from 2010

Where an ingredient or instruction was missing, I filled in what I thought each recipe left out and made my best guess about certain directions (what it means to age in a tin, or to roll to “exactly the right thickness”)
The recipes below are adapted from the originals, based on my own testing (I’ve indicated any discrepancies with the original recipes by adding “modified” to the ingredients list)
Here’s what happened—and my honest assessment of how it all tasted

title: Silicon Valley is Suffering From Model Collapse
excerpt: For anyone living outside Northern California, a lot of the messages coming out of Silicon Valley feel like they’ve been sent from another planet
body: For anyone living outside Northern California, a lot of the messages coming out of Silicon Valley feel like they’ve been sent from another planet

Last week, many of the industry’s top minds engaged in Olympic-level mental gymnastics as they defended the former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affairs: We must excuse his dalliances with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, they argued, not just because Huang is absolutely necessary to the American economy, which is being propped up by AI investment, but because we are in a geopolitical superintelligence race with China

Then this week, Anthropic, the company most vocally obsessed with the existential risk of AI, went public in an effort to raise $90 billion so that it could speed up construction of the very same systems it’s warning us about

How do we explain this pattern of illogical behavior? Maybe it’s standard avarice: Shareholders stand to make unfathomable amounts of money from Nvidia and Anthropic stock, and, ultimately, cash rules everything around me
But many Anthropic employees seem uninterested in the money
Maybe it’s a religious-level belief in the abundance of a future in which humans have ushered in superintelligence

Or maybe it’s the cult of the founder and a messianic sense of grandeur—the conviction that only those who see the future first in San Francisco can help protect us from the scourge of disease, from the Chinese, or from ourselves. [ Read: ] A $5.7 trillion face-plant But watching the AI doomerism on X, the lead-up to Anthropic’s IPO, and the fallout from Huang’s resignation, I think there’s a better framework for understanding what we’re seeing
The degradation of logic, the inscrutable decision making, and the bizarre detachment from popular opinion all point to a dynamic that the AI industry calls model collapse
The term describes a type of digital inbreeding that can theoretically occur when AI models train off synthetic AI output
The most influential figures in AI now sound as if they, having marinated in the insular worlds of the Bay Area and X, are suffering from their own version of the phenomenon
AI companies actually take pains to filter out AI slop when training their language models
You might call it circular reasoning, but the overall takeaway is the same: The corporate leaders shaping our future seem stuck in their own world
A recent post on a popular AI blog captures this spirit well, comparing AI-company employees to people who are microdosing psychedelics
These individuals appear as if they are “in a chronically mildly altered state of mind,” the post argues
Maybe, the post suggests, this state of mind allows them to “see some things more clearly” about AI models and their progress and capabilities than those of us on the outside
The downside, of course, is some form of inebriation
This is a helpful framework through which to view a lot of what’s coming out of the Bay Area
But there’s also a compounding effect: All day, every day, this culture talks with itself, its participants training on a recursive loop of information about the world and what they are building
This information bubble is self-reinforcing, frequently illogical, and also alienating
The Silicon Valley discourse about recursive self improvement in AI offers the best example of this degraded, circular reasoning

RSI refers to the concept of AI models improving themselves without human intervention or supervision, which would improve AI capabilities exponentially, accelerating discoveries in different fields and increasing the likelihood that models show signs of superintelligence and become far better than humans at any task they pursue

The downside of RSI, according to individuals including the Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, is that models “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems.” Humans would be flying blind and thus would likely rely more heavily on AI systems to interpret what is happening inside other AI systems
This is already happening to varying degrees when AI companies train and test new models, but RSI would speed it up to the point that humans would have fully relinquished control
This prospect seems to terrify many of the people who are closest to the technology. “There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI
Please look up!” Anna Wang, an alignment researcher at Anthropic, wrote this fall
Yet companies keep racing toward RSI out of fear that someone less principled will get there first

Anthropic argues that pushing forward with an eye toward AI safety will create a virtuous cycle of innovation—a “race to the top.” But you could just as easily argue that these companies are plowing ahead to justify and pay for hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure investments
Or that they are so deeply locked in competition with other AI companies and open models in China that they’re behaving irrationally
This September, Amodei wrote an essay arguing for a multilateral slowdown of AI development, a process he dubbed “pacing the frontier.” Ten days later, Anthropic released its newest model

Roughly a month later, in its IPO filing, the company confessed that its call to pace the frontier “does not describe our own model development or release timelines.” Sometimes, you can see the model collapse happening at an individual level—and it looks like naked hypocrisy
In September, an Anthropic researcher named Jacob Coxon quit the company in order to argue that AI companies might kill us all
He offered a heartfelt and convincing case in favor of taking the risk of human extinction seriously

But then, when asked in an interview that surfaced this week whether he would donate his OpenAI shares, he seemed to laugh off the suggestion that doing so would make any difference. “I like the money, bro,” he told the audience
Sigal Samuel, a writer who covers AI at Vox , has argued that at least some of this dynamic can be explained by a Silicon Valley culture steeped in effective altruism and rationalism
In this sphere, it’s not uncommon for adherents to justify huge risks using counterintuitive and dispassionate rationale
Some see this as a sophisticated form of argumentation, one that can eschew conventional morality (by risking rogue-AI swarm hacks or worse) for a greater purpose (achieving a technological utopia)

Samuel argues that the hyperrational thinking deployed by these leaders is overly clever. “Commonsense morality is actually often commonsense for a reason,” she told me recently. “And that’s because it tracks intuitions

Usually, reasoning like ‘If you don’t want a doom machine, don’t build a doom machine’ tends to be good reasoning.” Some who have quit the AI companies in protest describe the internal cultures as nonsensical, even schizophrenic, in nature

David Robinson, who wrote OpenAI’s transparency reports as a safety lead, argued in this publication that the company, which speaks obsessively about safety, approached AI development “with unimpeded optimism about being able to solve problems as they arise,” leading it to adopt a trial-and-error approach that is no longer responsible, given the power of its models
Relentless optimism is a necessary component of technological achievement but, as Robinson suggests, it can veer into hubris

title: Welcome to Software Beirut
excerpt: Last week, when it briefly looked like the world was collapsing while I sat on the tarmac, I wrote about the arrival of Software Beirut —“where nothing is broke
body: Last week, when it briefly looked like the world was collapsing while I sat on the tarmac, I wrote about the arrival of Software Beirut —“where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time, and the main skill you need is not being surprised.” I’m no Tom Friedman , but many people seemed to enjoy the phrase and encouraged me to keep using it even as outages at the FAA, Chase, and Microsoft proved to be isolated incidents unrelated to bad guys using advanced AI
Well, hold my mustache wax! Because I’m doubling down
The fact that all of the software chaos appears to have had boring causes doesn’t negate my point—it improves it

Software Beirut is not an event but an environment, shaped by three forces that arrived at roughly the same time: AI is exposing vulnerabilities in critical software at unprecedented speed; the rush to fix the bugs creates its own hair ball of risks and complications; and the federal government is gutting the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the department meant to coordinate the response, just as coordination matters most
The alarm first sounded in April, when Anthropic announced the existence of an AI model called Mythos that was the equivalent of X-ray glasses for software
Mythos could examine millions of lines of code and, in minutes, discover security flaws that had been invisible to human engineers for decades
Naturally, Mythos could also figure out how to exploit these flaws

Anthropic kept Mythos back from wide release, briefed the feds—including CISA—and gave some of the world’s biggest banks and tech and security companies early access so they could scan their own systems and get a head start on securing them
I’ve spoken with several IT executives who saw Mythos in that period
Each used their own signature compound profanity to express the mix of awe, professional jealousy, and shock at what Mythos could do
Their first thoughts were about the hacker networks and vandals who might use these new tools to wreak havoc on their institutions

They may still—especially as similar capabilities spread into freely available AI models. [ Josh Tyrangiel: The next major grounding will be worse ] But almost immediately, cyber defenders began a sprint to fix things that, until that day, they hadn’t known were broken
The scale of the repair effort is staggering

By July, 21 of the biggest software makers, including Microsoft, Google, and Apple, were disclosing about five times as many serious security vulnerabilities as their monthly record before Mythos, according to Epoch AI, a nonprofit research group
Microsoft released fixes for nearly 1,100 security vulnerabilities earlier this month, almost as many as it patched all of last year
Google has fixed more security bugs in two recent releases of its Chrome browser than in the previous 23 releases combined
Many of these flaws were discovered with the help of AI
Cool! But the repairs themselves can create new dangers
For decades, cybersecurity had a simple routine: Find a vulnerability, develop a patch, publish it, and give everyone time to install it
One cybersecurity executive told me his team can take a publicly released software fix and—thanks to the latest models—reverse-engineer it into a working exploit in under an hour
It tells the world exactly where the weakness is

Meanwhile, installing the fix, testing that the patch doesn’t break something else, and getting thousands of employees to reboot their laptops, all while communicating to customers and keeping regular service running—that’s human stuff
It’s infrastructure, and thinking about it like roads will help you understand the past week

Imagine if every road in the country were owned by a different person, each frantically sending out crews to fix potholes and set up detours on the same morning—and none of them talking to one another
But every one of those roads connects to roads that someone else owns
Wouldn’t it be great if somebody were in charge of coordinating all of the work? CISA is the closest thing we have to that
And here we arrive at some bitter calendar irony

Four days before the Mythos announcement, the Trump administration released its 2027 budget, which proposed cutting $700 million in programs from the cybersecurity agency, along with approximately 800 jobs
The agency has already lost about a third of its workforce since early 2025, and DOGE canceled contracts for teams that simulated attacks on government networks
Anyone who’s spent time in Lebanon might call this Beirut cosplay
A week of software outages and a government that shoots itself in the foot are a nice start, but the authentic experience requires one more ingredient: inequality
In Beirut, the prosperous have generators to insulate them from grid failures
In America, the same thing is happening with cyber defense
The Alliance for Critical Infrastructure , formed in February and expanded this fall, now includes nearly 50 American companies deemed vital across six sectors (Amazon, FedEx, Verizon, Citi)
The goal is to share knowledge and coordinate their cyber responses
Anthropic’s Project Glasswing is a similar club

We want these companies working together, and with the billions they already spend on security, they’re probably as prepared as anyone can be. [ Ian Bogost: What on earth is going on? ] But a private safety net is not a public one
School districts, local hospitals, city governments, and small businesses can’t possibly match the resources of these giants
A vandal looking to create chaos doesn’t need to risk taking on a bank when a county hospital runs on decades-old software and has one overworked IT person
This doesn’t mean the giants can afford to ignore the vulnerability of the little guys

title: The Download: a living liver, a billion-dollar battery deal, and AI hype

The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones
Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs

title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
excerpt: Record-breaking liver survival: A Sydney surgical team kept a human liver alive outside the body for seven weeks using an automated system of pumps and sensors
body: Record-breaking liver survival: A Sydney surgical team kept a human liver alive outside the body for seven weeks using an automated system of pumps and sensors that mimics the functions of a living body

Automation was the secret: When the team compared manual versus automated life-support systems across 55 donated livers, automated perfusion tripled average survival time to four weeks, with one organ reaching seven
Organs that heal: Organ perfusion has become more common over the past decade
Researchers have found some evidence that extended perfusion may allow damaged organs to repair themselves before transplant
A new frontier in medicine: Long-term organ life-support is attracting serious scientific interest

Two new scientific societies were recently founded to explore the concept. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148934" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.  In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System. “Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.    Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C
The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago
That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.  Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination
Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ
This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.  Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving
During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other

Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.   Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body

Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.   While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.” Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual
One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so

That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days —the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology
Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days
What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months

He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.   Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins , the Oklahoma surgeon

Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods
For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs
In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else
After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume
Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine

If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs. “It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”   He’s not the only one who thinks so
For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps
The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them
That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says
Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs , a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body

Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body
Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept
One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy

The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “ organ medicine” : research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”   “What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
excerpt: A billion-dollar battery deal: Sila, a US battery materials startup, has signed a major supply agreement with Panasonic Energy worth potentially over $1 billion
body: A billion-dollar battery deal: Sila, a US battery materials startup, has signed a major supply agreement with Panasonic Energy worth potentially over $1 billion, marking its first mass-market deal

Better batteries, lighter and faster: Sila's silicon-carbon anode material weighs a fifth as much as conventional graphite and cuts volume in half, enabling batteries that pack more energy, charge faster, and could extend EV range significantly

Geopolitics, not climate, is driving the money: With China controlling over 90% of graphite production, the Trump administration's Defense Department backed Sila with a $1.4 billion loan—framing batteries as a national security issue rather than a climate solution. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148922" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US
Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries
It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time
This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately
A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department
While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics
Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries
The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company
So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example
The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry
We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years
My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021
Things have gotten a lot bigger since then

In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain
The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating
But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.   This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years
Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech , have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year
The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics
While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics
China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today
For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals

But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it
Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition

Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.) I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority. “I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company
And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter
To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

title: A doctor’s guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP-1 medication
url:
<title>A doctor’s guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP-1 medication</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772854/original/file-20261118-64-kcnp5r.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C4000&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Alcohol can magnify GLP-1 drug side effects.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/celebratory-toast-for-thanksgiving-royalty-free-image/2176864678">filadendron/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends. </p>

<p>But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year. Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and cheese, decadent side dishes and an abundance of desserts.</p>

<p>For people taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes management, weight loss or other medical reasons, these celebrations can present unique challenges. Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the <a href="https://theconversation.com/dont-let-food-poisoning-crash-your-thanksgiving-dinner-269320">desire to maintain progress</a> can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://hospital.uillinois.edu/find-a-doctor/reed-berger-fleishman">physician specializing in obesity medicine</a>, I encourage my patients to view GLP-1 medications as an advantage during the holidays. These medications can help regulate appetite, improve awareness of fullness, and reinforce healthier eating behaviors during a season when food often takes center stage. </p>

<p>However, these medications don’t eliminate the possibility of overindulgence. In fact, patients who previously experienced little or no nausea due to GLP-1s may suddenly develop significant nausea or even vomiting after eating beyond their new comfort level. Nothing can <a href="https://theconversation.com/dont-let-food-poisoning-crash-your-thanksgiving-dinner-269320">derail a holiday celebration</a> quite like an upset stomach. Accounting for how these medications affect your body can help you avoid uncomfortable surprises while still enjoying the foods and traditions you love.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/LCcLPpO5drc?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">By quieting cravings, GLP-1 drugs can help people put tried and true dietary changes into practice.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>



<h2>Respecting fullness cues</h2>

<p>Whether taken by injection or orally, GLP-1 medications have become increasingly popular worldwide for managing <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21501-type-2-diabetes">Type 2 diabetes</a>, obesity and other chronic conditions. In the United States, <a href="http://dx.doi.org/10.15585/mmwr.mm7544a1">approximately 1 in 10 adults used these drugs</a> in 2025, and prescribing rates continue to climb.</p>

<p>GLP-1 medications work by reducing hunger, slowing stomach emptying and helping patients <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amjmed.2025.01.021">feel full sooner and stay full longer</a>. Many patients also report <a href="https://doi.org/doi:10.1016/j.obpill.2025.100181">fewer cravings for high-calorie foods</a> and even a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eclinm.2024.102920">reduced desire to drink alcohol</a>.</p>

<p>In many ways, these effects can make holiday food temptations easier to navigate. My patients often tell me that they already know which dietary changes they need to make, but GLP-1 medications help them put those changes into practice. They find it easier to stop eating when they’re satisfied, resist unnecessary snacking and avoid the constant thoughts about food that previously made weight management so challenging.</p>

<p>One of the most important things you can do during the holidays is to learn to recognize your body’s changing <a href="https://theconversation.com/our-sense-of-taste-helps-pace-our-eating-understanding-how-may-lead-to-new-avenues-for-weight-loss-220373">fullness signals</a>. Pay attention to nausea, bloating and early fullness rather than pushing yourself to finish everything on your plate. </p>

<p>These symptoms can serve as reminders that you’ve reached your comfortable limit. The best plan is to enjoy smaller portions, eat slowly and pause between bites to give your body time to recognize fullness. Rich, high-fat foods in particular can worsen nausea and prolong the sensation of fullness. A few bites of your favorite dishes may be much more satisfying than an entire serving.  </p>

<p>GLP-1 medications don’t make these decisions for you – but they can reinforce healthier behaviors.</p>

<h2>A caution on alcohol</h2>

<p>Alcohol deserves special consideration during the holidays, when social gatherings and <a href="https://theconversation.com/alcohol-is-one-of-the-most-dangerous-drugs-yet-its-presence-is-ubiquitous-in-social-settings-and-celebrations-278631">celebrations often revolve around drinking</a>. Although you may have tolerated alcohol without difficulty in the past, GLP-1 medications can change your experience.</p>

<p>Some patients report that GLP-1 medications <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eclinm.2024.102920">reduce their desire for alcohol</a> altogether. For them, the holidays may represent their first opportunity to drink since starting treatment.</p>

<p>Alcohol can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eclinm.2024.102920">worsen nausea, acid reflux, dehydration</a> and other gastrointestinal symptoms that some patients already experience while taking GLP-1 medications. If you choose to drink, consider these precautions:</p>

<ul>
<li><p>Limit your intake. Start with less than you might have consumed before starting your medication.</p></li>
<li><p>Avoid drinking on an empty stomach. Eat beforehand, but avoid a particularly large or high-fat meal.</p></li>
<li><p>Stay hydrated. Drink water throughout the occasion.</p></li>
<li><p>Pay attention to how you feel. Stop drinking if you experience nausea, dizziness or other unpleasant symptoms.</p></li>
</ul>

<p>The safest approach is to be cautious and recognize that alcohol can aggravate medication-related gastrointestinal symptoms. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772861/original/file-20261118-64-iaevop.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Man's hand holding a GLP-1 injection pen" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772861/original/file-20261118-64-iaevop.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772861/original/file-20261118-64-iaevop.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772861/original/file-20261118-64-iaevop.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772861/original/file-20261118-64-iaevop.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772861/original/file-20261118-64-iaevop.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772861/original/file-20261118-64-iaevop.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772861/original/file-20261118-64-iaevop.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Planning for travel</h2>

<p>Holiday travel can disrupt established routines, medication schedules and access to prescriptions. A little planning can help prevent unnecessary interruptions in treatment.</p>

<ul>
<li><p>Plan ahead for medication storage. Some injectable GLP-1 medications require refrigeration before use, while others allow room-temperature storage for a specified period after dispensing or first use. <a href="https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/215256s025lbl.pdf">Storage requirements vary</a> considerably by product. Check the prescribing information for your specific medication or ask your pharmacist before traveling. Don’t assume that all injectable medications can remain unrefrigerated for the same length of time.</p></li>
<li><p>If you’re flying, keep your medication and supplies in your carry-on luggage. This helps protect them from extreme temperatures and prevents problems if your checked luggage gets delayed or lost. Keep in mind that you might also need to have a note from your prescribing provider to carry them on.</p></li>
<li><p>Arrange prescription refills in advance. If you anticipate needing a refill while traveling, contact your pharmacy and prescribing clinician ahead of time. Prescribing and dispensing regulations can complicate obtaining medications in another state, so don’t wait until you run out.</p></li>
<li><p>Stick to your regular dosing schedule. Don’t take an extra dose or double up on medication to accommodate a holiday meal or try to suppress your appetite further. Taking more medication than prescribed can increase the risk of significant side effects and <a href="https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/glp-1-overdoses-rise-cause-concern-2026a1000dob">potentially cause an overdose</a>. If travel disrupts your dosing schedule or you miss a dose, follow the instructions for your specific medication, or contact your prescribing clinician or pharmacist.</p></li>
</ul>

<p>When in doubt, plan ahead and ask for guidance rather than making medication adjustments on your own.</p>

<h2>Don’t sweat it with the occasional treat</h2>

<p>Perhaps the most important advice I give my patients is this: The holidays are not everyday life, and one large meal or dessert will not erase the progress you’ve made.</p>

<p>You don’t need to skip Thanksgiving dinner, avoid your favorite dessert or feel guilty about enjoying a special meal. Maintaining a healthy relationship with food means allowing yourself flexibility while keeping your long-term goals in perspective.</p>

<p>At the same time, don’t let one celebratory meal turn into several weeks of abandoning the habits that have helped you succeed. Enjoy the occasion, recognize when you’ve had enough, and return to your usual routine afterward.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295301/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Alcohol can magnify GLP-1 drug side effects. filadendron/E+ via Getty Images Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends
But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year
Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and cheese, decadent side dishes and an abundance of desserts
For people taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes management, weight loss or other medical reasons, these celebrations can present unique challenges

Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different
As a physician specializing in obesity medicine , I encourage my patients to view GLP-1 medications as an advantage during the holidays
These medications can help regulate appetite, improve awareness of fullness, and reinforce healthier eating behaviors during a season when food often takes center stage
However, these medications don’t eliminate the possibility of overindulgence
In fact, patients who previously experienced little or no nausea due to GLP-1s may suddenly develop significant nausea or even vomiting after eating beyond their new comfort level
Nothing can derail a holiday celebration quite like an upset stomach
Accounting for how these medications affect your body can help you avoid uncomfortable surprises while still enjoying the foods and traditions you love
By quieting cravings, GLP-1 drugs can help people put tried and true dietary changes into practice
Respecting fullness cues Whether taken by injection or orally, GLP-1 medications have become increasingly popular worldwide for managing Type 2 diabetes , obesity and other chronic conditions
In the United States, approximately 1 in 10 adults used these drugs in 2025, and prescribing rates continue to climb
GLP-1 medications work by reducing hunger, slowing stomach emptying and helping patients feel full sooner and stay full longer
Many patients also report fewer cravings for high-calorie foods and even a reduced desire to drink alcohol
In many ways, these effects can make holiday food temptations easier to navigate
My patients often tell me that they already know which dietary changes they need to make, but GLP-1 medications help them put those changes into practice
They find it easier to stop eating when they’re satisfied, resist unnecessary snacking and avoid the constant thoughts about food that previously made weight management so challenging
One of the most important things you can do during the holidays is to learn to recognize your body’s changing fullness signals
Pay attention to nausea, bloating and early fullness rather than pushing yourself to finish everything on your plate
These symptoms can serve as reminders that you’ve reached your comfortable limit
The best plan is to enjoy smaller portions, eat slowly and pause between bites to give your body time to recognize fullness
Rich, high-fat foods in particular can worsen nausea and prolong the sensation of fullness
A few bites of your favorite dishes may be much more satisfying than an entire serving
GLP-1 medications don’t make these decisions for you – but they can reinforce healthier behaviors
A caution on alcohol Alcohol deserves special consideration during the holidays, when social gatherings and celebrations often revolve around drinking
Although you may have tolerated alcohol without difficulty in the past, GLP-1 medications can change your experience
Some patients report that GLP-1 medications reduce their desire for alcohol altogether
For them, the holidays may represent their first opportunity to drink since starting treatment
Alcohol can worsen nausea, acid reflux, dehydration and other gastrointestinal symptoms that some patients already experience while taking GLP-1 medications
If you choose to drink, consider these precautions: Limit your intake
Start with less than you might have consumed before starting your medication
Eat beforehand, but avoid a particularly large or high-fat meal
Stop drinking if you experience nausea, dizziness or other unpleasant symptoms

<title>Xi-Putin-Trump summit was heavy on symbolism, light on substance – and not exactly a Yalta II</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773074/original/file-20261119-64-eay814.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=2%2C0%2C5964%2C3976&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">China&#39;s Xi Jinping places himself firmly in the center of the trilateral summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/russian-president-vladimir-putin-president-of-china-xi-news-photo/2305850691?phrase=Trump%20Xi&amp;adppopup=true">Doug Mills/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>It was <a href="https://www.afp.com/en/china-us-russia-issue-declaration-toward-peace-after-first-summit">touted as a history-making</a> summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the <a href="https://apnews.com/article/apec-economy-china-trump-xi-putin-asia-bb61e50e4b0bb0b975b0695dc4f7b64a">Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit</a>, for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders.</p>

<p>Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/ukraine-invasion-2022-117045">ongoing war in Ukraine</a>, <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/iran-war-185765">Middle East conflict</a> and the <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/artificial-intelligence-ai-90">march of artificial intelligence technology</a> chief among them.</p>

<p>But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver? </p>

<p>As an <a href="https://www.hks.harvard.edu/faculty/rana-mitter">expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School</a>, I saw a lot of style, but less substance.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773079/original/file-20261119-64-u3ilsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Three men in suits shake hands" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773079/original/file-20261119-64-u3ilsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773079/original/file-20261119-64-u3ilsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773079/original/file-20261119-64-u3ilsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773079/original/file-20261119-64-u3ilsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773079/original/file-20261119-64-u3ilsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773079/original/file-20261119-64-u3ilsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773079/original/file-20261119-64-u3ilsz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping looks on in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-donald-trump-shakes-hands-with-russian-president-news-photo/2305167096?phrase=Trump%20Xi&amp;adppopup=true">Iori Sagisawa/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What were the key takeaways from the meeting?</h2>

<p>The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order.</p>

<p>And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-18/china-s-xi-greets-trump-at-airport-in-shenzhen-in-rare-move">he was met by Xi</a>. Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president.</p>

<p>And <a href="https://www.axios.com/2026/11/18/trump-china-xi-hug-airport">then came a hug</a> – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773123/original/file-20261119-62-k7w0bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two men embrace at the bottom of red stairs." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773123/original/file-20261119-62-k7w0bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773123/original/file-20261119-62-k7w0bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773123/original/file-20261119-62-k7w0bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773123/original/file-20261119-62-k7w0bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773123/original/file-20261119-62-k7w0bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773123/original/file-20261119-62-k7w0bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773123/original/file-20261119-62-k7w0bv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A rare airport hug from Xi Jinping.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/president-donald-trump-is-greeted-by-chinas-president-xi-news-photo/2305160371?phrase=Trump%20Xi%20airport&amp;adppopup=true">Mandel Ngan/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/18/world/trump-xi-putin-apec">big table with Trump, Putin and Xi</a> there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China <a href="https://archive-yaleglobal.yale.edu/content/under-xi-china-aims-be-worlds-middle-kingdom">presenting as the “Middle Kingdom</a>,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen.</p>

<p>In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds.</p>

<p>So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/chinas-expanding-influence-at-the-united-nations-and-how-the-united-states-should-react/">wants more power</a> in the organization, while <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/trumps-criticism-un">Trump has become increasingly disillusioned</a> with the international body.</p>

<p>And there was also a lot of <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/no-breakthroughs-from-trump-xi-and-putins-3-way-talks-on-nuclear-risks">discussion on nuclear weapons controls</a>. In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev <a href="https://vanguardeast.com/nuclear-war-cannot-be-won-must-never-be-fought/">first aired in 1985</a>: “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.”</p>

<p>All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/nukes-without-limits-a-new-era-after-the-end-of-new-start">expired a while ago</a>, and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter.</p>

<h2>What wasn’t discussed?</h2>

<p>The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations.</p>

<p>For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has <a href="https://www.foxnews.com/politics/trump-keeps-signaling-end-iran-war-expert-warns-crucial-piece-his-strategy-missing">not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion</a> some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged.</p>

<p>But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting.</p>

<p>At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi. </p>

<p>Beyond those conflicts, <a href="https://www.economist.com/china/2026/03/24/chinas-government-both-drives-and-constrains-the-rise-of-ai">AI regulation</a> and <a href="https://atlasinstitute.org/critical-minerals-supply-chains-us-china/">critical mineral supply chains</a> were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>This was touted as Yalta II – was it?</h2>

<p>There <a href="https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/why--yalta-2--is-exactly-the-right-analogy-for-a-trump-putin-xi-summit">were some immediate similarities</a> with the <a href="https://history.state.gov/milestones/1937-1945/yalta-conf">Yalta Conference</a> – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table.  </p>

<p>Of course, the big three then included Britain; there was no China. That alone tells you how much geopolitics has changed over 80 years.</p>

<p>Also, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill were all on the same side in 1945. It was a case of comrades in arms that would soon be drifting apart as the Cold War developed.</p>

<p>Here it may well be the other way around. China and Russia are partners, but the U.S. is seen as their adversary.</p>

<p>What Trump may want is detente rather than a new Cold War. Does this mean an emerging policy of Russia, China and the U.S. coming together in a new order? I imagine the Europeans may have something to say about that.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297087/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
