Doug Mills/Getty Images It was touted as a history-making summit of the year

Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit , for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders
Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine , Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them
But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver? As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School , I saw a lot of style, but less substance
President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping looks on in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18, 2026
Iori Sagisawa/AFP via Getty Images What were the key takeaways from the meeting? The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion

And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order
And this was on show even before the leaders sat down
At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi
Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president
And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented
I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades
Mandel Ngan/Getty Images It was all choreographed, of course
The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic
Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom ,” steadying the world
Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen
In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds
So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done
In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body
And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls
In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats
Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S

President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985 : “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.” All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented
The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago , and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter
What wasn’t discussed? The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations
Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began
The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged
But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end
In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting
At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine
It was not mentioned by name at the summit

Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi
Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders
But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen
It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings

President Franklin Roosevelt and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin sit together at the Yalta Conference

Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe

<h2>What the court ruled</h2>

<p>Gambia’s case focused on actions that Myanmar’s military government called “clearance operations” in the course of its decades-long violent persecution of the country’s <a href="https://www.nationalgeographic.com/culture/article/rohingya-people">Muslim Rohingya minority</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-56660483">The Tatmadaw</a>, as the Myanmar military is known, justified these actions as a counterinsurgency operation. Yet in the course of those attacks, soldiers were found to have <a href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/press-release/2017/09/who-are-the-rohingya-and-why-are-they-fleeing-myanmar/">destroyed hundreds of Rohingya villages</a>, and to have committed widespread rapes, torture and summary killings. </p>

<p>While the precise death toll of the 2017 attacks may never be known, at least 10,000 Rohingya civilians <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/hague-icj-court-myanmar-rohingya-ruling-9.7427764">are thought to have died</a>, and roughly 750,000 Rohingya fled to neighboring Bangladesh. There they joined other Rohingya in what is now the <a href="https://www.unhcr.org/where-we-work/countries/bangladesh">world’s largest refugee camp</a> of over 1.2 million people, comprised of those who had already fled years of the Myanmar government’s persecution and attacks.</p>

<p>The court’s ruling that the Tatmadaw’s attacks amounted to genocide rested on its interpretation of the crime of genocide in the <a href="https://ihl-databases.icrc.org/en/ihl-treaties/genocide-conv-1948">1948 U.N. Genocide Convention</a>, the first major international treaty approved by the United Nations General Assembly. </p>

<p>For an attack to be genocidal, it must be directed against an ethnic, religious, racial or national group, and must include at least one of five prohibited acts: killing members of a group; inflicting serious physical or mental harm on members; deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about its destruction; imposing measures intended to prevent births; or forcibly transferring children from the group. </p>

<p>Beyond these factual requirements, genocide requires that the perpetrator specifically intended these acts to destroy the group, in whole or in part. </p>

<p><iframe id="Jwmm4" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Jwmm4/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Map of Myanmar"></iframe></p>

<p>In its ruling, the court agreed that the facts of Myanmar’s attacks met the legal definition of genocide. For the notoriously difficult and demanding requirement for proving the “<a href="https://www.un.org/en/genocide-prevention/definition">special intent</a>” to destroy a group, the court determined that the pattern, selective targeting and lethality of the attacks on Rohingya villages could not plausibly be explained as a counterinsurgency operation. </p>

<p>Instead, the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the military’s actions, the court determined, was the specific intent to destroy the Rohingya ethnic minority.</p>

<h2>A series of historic firsts</h2>

<p>The court’s decision is unprecedented in many important respects. </p>

<p>In an influential <a href="https://www.icj-cij.org/case/91/judgments">previous ruling</a> on violations of the Genocide Convention, in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro in 2007, the court found only that Serbia had not met its legal duty to prevent genocide by failing to use its influence to restrain the Bosnian Serb army in the <a href="https://www.un.org/en/observances/srebrenica-genocide-commemoration-day/about">Srebrenica massacre of 1995</a>.</p>

<p>In the Myanmar ruling, by contrast, the court ruled for the first time that a country is legally responsible for committing genocide – not merely failing to prevent it.</p>

<p>Further, the court ruled for the first time that a country that has committed genocide also has multiple obligations toward the victim group. Those include designing and implementing a comprehensive program of reparations and compensation for victims; creating conditions where Rohingya can make a safe, voluntary and dignified return to their homes; and restoration of their citizenship status after national legislation from 1982 <a href="https://www.migrationpolicy.org/journal/feature/stateless-and-persecuted-what-next-rohingya">rendered them stateless</a>.</p>

<p>Finally, the court also demanded that Myanmar take steps to investigate all those involved in the genocide to determine individual criminal responsibility. Since the International Court of Justice is not a criminal court and only hears cases between states, this order explicitly connects the ruling to other courts where individual perpetrators can be held accountable. </p>

<p>These include the International Criminal Court – which had <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2024/11/1157536">already requested an arrest warrant</a> for Tatmadaw leader Min Aung Hlaing – as well as national courts that may pursue prosecution according to the doctrine of universal jurisdiction.</p>

<h2>The ruling’s broader implications</h2>

<p>The court’s ruling in Gambia vs. Myanmar is also likely to have huge ramifications far beyond the case itself. </p>

<p>In filing its complaint, Gambia appealed to an innovative argument to establish that it had legal standing. It argued for what’s known as “<a href="https://www.law.georgetown.edu/international-law-journal/wp-content/uploads/sites/21/2021/06/GT-GJIL210018.pdf">erga omnes partes</a>,” roughly translated as “toward all parties to a treaty.” According to this line of reasoning, the Genocide Convention imposes such strong legal duties to prevent and punish the crime of genocide that any state, even one that has not in any way been directly harmed, has the standing – in fact, the obligation – to seek legal remedies. </p>

<p>In accepting Gambia’s “erga omnes partes” approach, the court opened a pathway for other cases centering on violations of the Genocide Convention. Of these, the most significant by far is the ongoing case of <a href="https://www.icj-cij.org/case/192">South Africa v. Israel</a>, which charges the Israeli government and the Israeli military of committing genocide against Palestinian civilians in the Gaza Strip. Going forward, other nations would now also have a legal tool for holding perpetrator states accountable for committing the most serious international crimes.</p>

<p>The International Court of Justice has no enforcement arm. As such, the Myanmar government cannot be compelled to abide by its rulings, whether to cease any further attacks or persecution on the Rohingya, make efforts to repatriate them or design a comprehensive reparation and compensation plan. </p>

<p>But even if Myanmar chooses to ignore the court’s specific orders, the ruling is a major defeat. The reputational damage of being the first country found guilty of state-sponsored genocide is likely to be considerable. Further, the ruling will <a href="https://specialadvisorycouncil.org/2026/09/navigating-the-forthcoming-icj-judgment-in-the-gambia-v-myanmar-a-roadmap-for-member-states/">support claims</a> that other nations have a duty not to assist Myanmar in any way that might support or enable further attacks on Rohingya. </p>

<p>While that doesn’t automatically mean other countries will fulfill their duties under international law, many are nonetheless likely to use the ruling to bolster multilateral efforts to impose political, economic and social costs on the Tatmadaw. That could include targeted economic sanctions, financial restrictions, prohibitions on arms sales and other forms of cooperation with Myanmar’s government. The ruling thus comes with a potentially hefty price tag for the military junta. </p>

<p>Given the general <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/law/2025/jun/26/are-we-witnessing-the-death-of-international-law">weakening of international legal institutions</a> over the past 20 years, a <a href="https://www.economist.com/by-invitation/2025/06/24/the-uns-dysfunction-undermines-global-security-argue-ban-ki-moon-and-helen-clark">dysfunctional U.N. Security Council</a> and an <a href="https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/trump-icc-sanctions-war-crimes/">International Criminal Court under siege by the Trump administration</a>, the court’s ruling is a rare victory for international justice and opens new routes for international genocide prevention and accountability efforts.</p>

            </figcaption>

<p>Before all else, though, it is also a victory for the Rohingya – a people who have suffered decades of persecution.</p>

<p>Thousands gathered in their Bangladeshi refugee camps to watch and cheer as the court’s president, Judge Iwasawa Yuji, read the court’s judgment. Camp inhabitants held aloft signs and <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/19/world/myanmar-icj-ruling-genocide">chanted a simple message</a> as the verdict came down: “Thank you Gambia.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296987/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

It argued for what’s known as “ erga omnes partes ,” roughly translated as “toward all parties to a treaty.” According to this line of reasoning, the Genocide Convention imposes such strong legal duties to prevent and punish the crime of genocide that any state, even one that has not in any way been directly harmed, has the standing – in fact, the obligation – to seek legal remedies
In accepting Gambia’s “erga omnes partes” approach, the court opened a pathway for other cases centering on violations of the Genocide Convention
Of these, the most significant by far is the ongoing case of South Africa v
Israel , which charges the Israeli government and the Israeli military of committing genocide against Palestinian civilians in the Gaza Strip
Going forward, other nations would now also have a legal tool for holding perpetrator states accountable for committing the most serious international crimes
The International Court of Justice has no enforcement arm

As such, the Myanmar government cannot be compelled to abide by its rulings, whether to cease any further attacks or persecution on the Rohingya, make efforts to repatriate them or design a comprehensive reparation and compensation plan

<title>US and Iran once practiced diplomacy through archaeology – that legacy need not lie in ruins</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772848/original/file-20261118-64-zu3031.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C123%2C5815%2C3877&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A damaged carving inside the Golestan Palace in Tehran, Iran.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/damaged-carving-can-be-seen-during-a-press-tour-of-golestan-news-photo/2263990043?phrase=Golestan%20Palace&amp;adppopup=true">Majid Saeedi/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>When a U.S. airstrike <a href="https://www.the-independent.com/news/world/middle-east/iran-golestan-palace-damaged-airstrike-us-israel-war-b2930842.html">struck Tehran’s Arg Square</a> on March 2, 2026, Golestan Palace was not the target. But it was close enough. </p>

<p>The missile’s impact blew out windows across the palace complex and damaged some of its elaborate 19th-century interiors. In <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/golestan-palace-iran-strikes-damage-photos-2026-3">photographs taken afterward</a>, pieces of its celebrated mirrorwork lay scattered across the floor.</p>

<p>Golestan is a <a href="https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1422/">UNESCO World Heritage Site</a> and one of the great surviving monuments of Iran’s Qajar dynasty, which ruled from 1789 until 1925. Within hours of the strike, <a href="https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-expresses-concern-over-protection-cultural-heritage-sites-amidst-escalating-violence-middle?hub=80094">UNESCO reported the damage</a> and noted that cultural property is protected under international law during armed conflict. </p>

<p>The palace was not only an early casualty of the U.S.-Iran war, but a symbolically potent one, too. And as my colleague Mehrnoush Soroush at the Center for Ancient Middle Eastern Landscapes <a href="https://heritagewatch.camelab.net/">has documented</a>, Golestan is not alone. Since the war in Iran began in February 2026, reports of <a href="https://the-european.eu/story-68260/irans-historic-treasures-face-destruction-as-war-puts-centuries-of-heritage-at-risk.html">damage to heritage sites have poured in</a> from all across Iran.</p>

<p><iframe id="tc-infographic-1367" class="tc-infographic" height="400px" src="https://cdn.theconversation.com/infographics/1367/1fd8912b76476357984574fe185de53dbdb4d55d/site/index.html" width="100%" style="border: none" frameborder="0" title="Interactive map of damaged heritage sites in Iran"></iframe></p>

<p>I know that damaged buildings — no matter how valuable — cannot compare with the human costs of war. But the images from Golestan have particular resonance to me, an archaeologist who <a href="https://anthropology.washu.edu/people/kyle-g-olson">studies the history of relations between Iran and the United States</a>. It also cuts against a history of cooperation between American and Iranian archaeologists, in which Americans worked to preserve, rather than destroy, Iranian heritage.</p>

<h2>Digging in, together</h2>

<p>I have spent years researching how archaeologists, museums and cultural officials from the two countries worked together before the <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-iranian-revolution-a-timeline-of-events/">Iranian Revolution of 1979</a>. </p>

<p>My <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/02757206.2023.2261972">earlier research has examined</a> how archaeology became entangled with American foreign aid and Iranian development programs during the 1960s, and I am currently writing a book on the history of U.S.-Iranian heritage diplomacy over the past century.</p>

<p>I believe that history offers another way of thinking about what has been lost in the current conflict. Long before Iran and the U.S. became adversaries, cultural heritage provided a setting in which people from the two countries learned how to work together.</p>

<p>American archaeologists <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/uk/americaniranian-dialogues-9781350118720/">began excavating in Iran in the early 1930s</a>. In those days, the relationship was unequal: American museums sought access to archaeological sites and, under agreements with the Iranian government, received portions of the objects they excavated under the <a href="https://smarthistory.org/partage/">colonial system of partage</a>. As a result, <a href="https://collections.penn.museum/collections/search.php?term=iran&amp;submit_term=Submit">museums</a> across the U.S. still hold substantial collections of Iranian antiquities.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A black-and-white photo shows an excavated site." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772892/original/file-20261118-64-lybjwp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772892/original/file-20261118-64-lybjwp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=282&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772892/original/file-20261118-64-lybjwp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=282&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772892/original/file-20261118-64-lybjwp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=282&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772892/original/file-20261118-64-lybjwp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=354&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772892/original/file-20261118-64-lybjwp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=354&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772892/original/file-20261118-64-lybjwp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=354&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The site of an archeological dig at Hasanlu, Iran.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hasanloo2.jpg">Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The terms of the relationship changed considerably during the 1960s, as the U.S. and Iran intensified their connections. At the same time that thousands of American professionals, educators, businesspeople, scholars and others came to work and live in Iran, the country <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/1743873X.2022.2096457">revised its antiquities laws and expanded its own archaeological institutions, universities and museums</a>, resulting in, among other things, <a href="https://ajammc.com/2023/07/14/destination-persia-tourism-1960s/">a major tourism boom</a>. </p>

<p>American archaeologists still wanted permission to dig at Iranian sites, but they increasingly operated within a system controlled by Iranian officials. In return, American institutions contributed funding and access to laboratories, specialist knowledge, graduate education and connections to an international scholarly community.</p>

<p>American archaeological projects in Iran drew on large networks of such connections. Scholars <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/book/81281">working on the Deh Luran Plain</a> in southwestern Iran, for example, depended on Iranian government agencies, the U.S. Embassy, American universities and museums, development organizations and scientific laboratories. Botanical remains, animal bones and other materials moved through specialist laboratories abroad, while Iranian officials worked alongside foreign researchers in the field.</p>

<h2>Collaboration under the shah</h2>

<p>By the 1970s, <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003224129">fieldwork projects</a> were increasingly becoming joint enterprises, based on formal partnerships between institutions and cooperative leadership. Iranian archaeological authorities employed American specialists to help <a href="https://press.umich.edu/Books/A/Archaeological-Investigations-in-Northeastern-Xuzestan-1976">survey areas threatened by dams and other development projects</a>, while Iranian archaeologists increasingly took leading roles in the field. Meanwhile, students moved in greater numbers between Tehran, Chicago, Philadelphia and New York. Museums organized <a href="https://www.artforum.com/features/iranian-art-211785/">traveling exhibitions</a>, and Iran hosted <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/469523400">international scholarly congresses</a> devoted to its history and archaeology.</p>

<p>It can’t be ignored that these collaborations flourished during a period when Iran, under Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, <a href="https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/taken-hostage-presidents-shah-strategic-partnership/">was a close American ally</a>. </p>

<p>While the terms of the relationship increasingly favored Iran, they were still marked by geopolitical inequalities. American universities and museums possessed resources that Iranian institutions often lacked – not only financially and in terms of human capital, but physically, in the form of collections of artifacts that had previously been taken out of Iran.</p>

<p>Yet the collaborations also developed lives of their own, as American scholars returned year after year.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772864/original/file-20261118-64-fdcgqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two people walk around some ancient ruins." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772864/original/file-20261118-64-fdcgqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772864/original/file-20261118-64-fdcgqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772864/original/file-20261118-64-fdcgqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772864/original/file-20261118-64-fdcgqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772864/original/file-20261118-64-fdcgqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772864/original/file-20261118-64-fdcgqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772864/original/file-20261118-64-fdcgqa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The archeological site at Persepolis, Iran, in 1976.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Found_Photo_-_Iran_-_Persepolis_-_Archeological_Site_12.tif_(33630141871).jpg">Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Post-revolutionary changes</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-iranian-revolution-a-timeline-of-events/">Islamic Revolution</a> exposed both how extensive and fragile this network was. Even as the crisis that began in 1978 deepened, American archaeologists did not initially assume that their Iranian partnerships were finished. At Malyan, the remains of ancient Anshan, <a href="https://commons.library.stonybrook.edu/amar/157/">archaeologist William Sumner</a> proposed continuing to pay a watchman to protect the site, while maintaining contact with Iranian colleagues so research could eventually resume. </p>

<p>That did not come to pass. And much of the American-Iranian archaeological enterprise collapsed as diplomatic relations between the two countries soured after the Islamic Republic took 52 American diplomats and civilians <a href="https://history.state.gov/departmenthistory/short-history/iraniancrises">hostage in 1979</a> and Washington sided with Baghdad during the <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/Iran-Iraq-War">Iran-Iraq War</a> in the 1980s.</p>

<p>But the example of the 1960s and ‘70s points toward a sometimes less visible part of diplomacy: relationships accumulated through repeated practical work. </p>

<p>International relations expert Trita Parsi makes this point in his history of the negotiations that produced the <a href="https://www.cfr.org/backgrounders/what-iran-nuclear-deal">2015 Iran nuclear agreement</a>. In “<a href="https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300218169/losing-an-enemy/">Losing an Enemy</a>,” based on interviews with participants on both sides, Parsi describes the working relationship that developed between U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif. </p>

<p>This is not to say that their personal rapport produced the nuclear agreement by itself. Naturally, presidents had to authorize negotiations, diplomats at all levels had to find compromises, and both governments had to conclude that an agreement served their interests. But <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/how-john-and-javad-learned-to-work-together-on-an-iran-deal/2015/07/03/c1dd3ffa-cb17-40c3-ac37-a97c4f495b65_story.html">contemporary reporting</a> described that relationship as one built on professional respect and repeated close proximity. In other words, Kerry and Zarif spent enough time negotiating together to understand each other’s constraints and establish a working relationship despite the hostility between their two governments.</p>

<p>That kind of personal working relationship can assist diplomacy – not just at the highest levels but more broadly across civil society. <a href="https://www.state.gov/sports-diplomacy">Sports diplomacy</a> has long been acknowledged; so too the <a href="https://www.history.com/articles/panda-diplomacy-the-worlds-cutest-ambassadors">sharing of zoological “gifts.”</a> My research shows that archaeology has long had an important a place in these kinds of cultural exchanges as well.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A group of men hold photos of damaged buildings" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772851/original/file-20261118-64-4xekh2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772851/original/file-20261118-64-4xekh2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772851/original/file-20261118-64-4xekh2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772851/original/file-20261118-64-4xekh2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772851/original/file-20261118-64-4xekh2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772851/original/file-20261118-64-4xekh2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772851/original/file-20261118-64-4xekh2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Iranians gather on April 4, 2026, to protest strikes on Iran’s historic sites.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/group-of-cultural-heritage-lovers-gather-to-condemn-the-news-photo/2269163625?phrase=Golestan%20Palace&amp;adppopup=true">Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Today, Iranian conservation specialists are sorting and cataloging shattered fragments from Golestan Palace while attempting to <a href="https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/09/04/irans-heritage-experts-race-to-repair-damaged-sites-as-negotiations-stall">repair damage at heritage sites around the country</a>.</p>

<p>At the same time, American and Iranian officials are still looking for ways to end the conflict. I don’t know what U.S.-Iranian relations will look like when the fighting eventually ends, but damaged buildings and monuments will need to be repaired and conserved. If my inbox is anything to go by, Iranian scholars still want to work together with American colleagues. </p>

<p>And if a larger political opening for U.S.-Iranian rapprochement ever arrives, the relationships built by those who steward and study Iran’s heritage may matter more than they first appear.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292886/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Nvidia isn’t the first company to dump a misbehaving CEO – history shows it’s in the interest of corporate boards to act

<title>Nvidia isn’t the first company to dump a misbehaving CEO – history shows it’s in the interest of corporate boards to act</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772853/original/file-20261118-64-1rqnfu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7488%2C4992&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Nvidia&#39;s board is now coming under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted its CEO, Jensen Huang.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/co-founder-president-and-ceo-of-us-technology-company-news-photo/2299493247?phrase=nvidia%20board%20directors&amp;adppopup=true">Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis.</p>

<p>This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/nvidia-is-preparing-to-oust-nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-30f421ad">ouster of its CEO</a>, Jensen Huang. But it <a href="https://knowledge.insead.edu/leadership-organisations/mark-hurd-affair">actually transpired over 15 years ago</a> at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd.</p>

<p>Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/17/nvidia-jensen-huang-succession-board-lessons.html">shifting from his behavior to his board</a> – and the decisions that led to his exit. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.wsj.com/tech/the-campaign-to-bring-back-jensen-huang-as-nvidia-ceo-e91b0b2c">Prominent industry leaders</a> <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/nvidias-board-not-considering-reinstating-jensen-huang-as-ceo-a2b913b1">are questioning</a> the board’s decision to oust him. <a href="https://www.cbc.ca/news/business/nvidia-ceo-huang-calls-reinstatements-9.7423555">They include</a> Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Meanwhile, an internal petition allegedly signed by more than 1,600 Nvidia employees <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/nvidia-employees-petition-for-jensen-huangs-return/">has also called</a> for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Ba6zwJQAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">scholar of management</a> who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board made the right call. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, <a href="https://doi.org/10.5465/AMBPP.2017.16401abstract">I have repeatedly found</a> that doing nothing, as a board, <a href="https://oaktrust.library.tamu.edu/items/18703a1c-50be-4f9b-aa94-016212e01ddf">is worse</a> than doing something.</p>

<p>CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. </p>

<p>But <a href="https://hbr.org/2026/11/how-boards-detect-and-prevent-internal-misconduct">it’s still hard</a> for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. If the board is <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/how-nvidias-board-made-billions-while-overseeing-the-company-0473818c">earning billions</a>, it’s even more difficult.</p>

<h2>The costs of misconduct</h2>

<p>One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct <a href="https://oaktrust.library.tamu.edu/items/18703a1c-50be-4f9b-aa94-016212e01ddf">exit at a significantly higher rate</a> than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because <a href="https://oaktrust.library.tamu.edu/items/18703a1c-50be-4f9b-aa94-016212e01ddf">they’re forced out</a> due to poor performance, my research shows. </p>

<p>One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/best-buy-founder-resigns-as-chairman-after-ceo-probe/">stepped down as chairman</a> of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it.</p>

<p>Directors are also <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/01492063231225420">personally penalized</a> for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may <a href="https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2006.23478165">lose their board seats</a> or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct <a href="https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2008.32626007">may spill over</a> to damage the reputations of those companies as well. </p>

<p>In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. </p>

<p>In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/17/nvidia-creates-board-committee-to-oversee-export-controls">potential national security risks</a>.</p>

<p>Another issue is <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/moral-hazard">moral hazard</a>: when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation.</p>

<p>My research has found that risk to be high. </p>

<p>When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance <a href="https://hdl.handle.net/1969.1/156941">is often even worse</a> than the first.  </p>

<p>Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2007/02/11/us-airways-ceo-had-previous-drunk-driving-incidents-report.html">prompting criticism of the board</a> for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Then-American Airlines CEO Doug Parker speaks behind a microphone as he testifies before senators on December 15, 2021, in Washington, DC" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772860/original/file-20261118-64-8g54ty.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="caption">Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/american-airlines-ceo-doug-parker-testifies-before-the-news-photo/1237251103?phrase=American%20Airlines%20CEO%20Doug%20Parker&amp;adppopup=true">CHIP SOMODEVILLA/POOL/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/why-do-boards-keep-giving-misbehaving-ceos-second-chances-228db0b7">recently ousted</a> as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship.</p>

<p>In the case of Nvidia, Jensen <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-board.html">reportedly lied</a> to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future?  </p>

<h2>A question of culture</h2>

<p>Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. </p>

<p>CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s <a href="https://hdl.handle.net/1969.1/156941">often associated</a> with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive.</p>

<p>Take <a href="https://www.wsj.com/articles/american-apparel-gets-restraining-order-against-ex-ceo-charney-1433246872">Dov Charney’s tenure</a> as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees.</p>

<p>It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct.</p>

<p>For now, the public debate has largely centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight.</p>

<p>It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor <a href="https://hbr.org/2026/11/how-boards-detect-and-prevent-internal-misconduct">Warren Buffett noted</a>: “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296800/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Eurovision took its song contest to Asia – bringing its political drama and cultural tropes along for the ride</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772838/original/file-20261118-64-8g6f2t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3999%2C2666&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Laos&#39; contestant, Thinla, performs at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 in Bangkok on Nov. 14, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/laos-contestant-thinla-performs-during-the-grand-final-of-news-photo/2304598177?adppopup=true">Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfYp3HLHuA4">ABBA</a> and <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VXLWfXmlXPc">Céline Dion</a> came to the world’s attention thanks to the Eurovision Song Contest, an annual showcase of pop music, camp and spectacle. </p>

<p>Filipino singer Carmelle is hoping that the Eurovision Song Contest Asia will serve as a similar springboard to international fame. On Nov. 14, 2026, Carmelle bested entries from 11 Asian countries <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/world/asia-eurovision">to be crowned the Asian edition’s first-ever winner</a>. The competition marked Eurovision’s boldest expansion of its format in its 70-year history.</p>

<p>As a scholar of <a href="https://online.ucpress.edu/jpms/article/37/3/21/213486/Everybody-Wanna-Move-Like-Us-Performing-Afro">contemporary European popular music and politics</a>, I study the ways in which Eurovision shapes notions of what it looks like and sounds like to be European. Knowing that the Asian edition would be organized by European broadcasting executives, I wanted to see how closely Eurovision Asia would resemble the flagship Eurovision, or whether it would carve out an identity of its own.</p>

<h2>Stops and starts</h2>

<p>Eurovision’s proposed expansion into Asia dates back to 2008, when the European Broadcasting Union – the transnational coalition of public service media organizations that has organized the Eurovision Song Contest since 1956 – announced plans for “<a href="https://eurovoix.com/our-sound-asia-pacific-song-contest/">Our Sound – The Asia-Pacific Song Contest</a>.” Originally slated to debut in 2010, the project never materialized.</p>

<p>On March 31, 2026, however, Voxovation, a European-led production company that oversees the development of Eurovision’s spinoffs, announced <a href="https://www.ebu.ch/news/2026/03/bangkok-to-host-first-ever-eurovision-song-contest-asia-in-2026">that Bangkok would host</a> the inaugural Asian competition in partnership with Thailand’s Channel 3 and S2O Productions.</p>

<p>Eurovision Asia is now the second European Broadcasting Union-licensed global spinoff to make the airwaves. </p>

<p>In 2022, Voxovation organized <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/despite-a-michael-bolton-performance-american-song-contest-fails-to-fulfill-its-campy-eurovision-042532335.html">the American Song Contest</a>, which included original songs by artists from all 50 U.S. states, five territories and Washington. </p>

<p>Despite being promoted to the American public in a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TgHgsZ0AXlE">Super Bowl commercial</a> featuring hosts Kelly Clarkson and Snoop Dogg, the competition <a href="https://www.escunited.com/the-american-song-contest-not-renewed-for-2023-hope-remains-for-2024-return/">failed to attract a large viewership</a> and the spinoff wasn’t renewed.</p>

<h2>‘You will be blown away!’</h2>

<p>Given two decades of uncertainty, as well as the failure of Voxovation’s U.S. spinoff, some critics doubted whether the Asian version would succeed. And for a moment, it looked like everything might fall apart: In late October 2026, <a href="https://www.aftonbladet.se/nojesbladet/melodifestivalen/a/Wg1mOr/uppgifter-kris-for-ebu-s-eurovision-satsning-i-asien">the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet</a> reported that Eurovision Asia’s original budget of approximately US$4.5 million had been reduced by US$1 million.</p>

<p>The European Broadcasting Union, however, confirmed that the show would go on as planned, and at 8:30 p.m. Bangkok time on Nov. 14, the show’s two hosts, Thai media personalities Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop, welcomed viewers from around the world tuning in via television broadcast and the YouTube livestream.</p>

<p>“Maybe you’ve never heard of Eurovision before, or maybe you’re one of the hardcore Eurofans,” said Bishop. “It doesn’t matter, because you will be blown away by the talent here tonight!”</p>

<p>For the next two-and-a-half hours, each country’s representative performed an original song, with Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên opening the show with her song “Em Tiên” (“Fairy Maiden”).</p>

<p>Vietnam’s entry had many of the spectacular ingredients of an ideal Eurovision entry: bilingual lyrics, large props, flashy outfits and a dance break. The song’s instrumentation included a flute accompanying Tiên’s melody and a bamboo xylophone. It concluded with a second, high-energy dance break reminiscent of electronic dance music genres.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/4flXEWQe_rs?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Vietnam’s live performance at Eurovision Asia 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The song’s use of traditional Asian musical signifiers followed the approach of the European entrants that <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/book/68106">have incorporated folk traditions</a> to promote their national cultures to an international audience.</p>

<p>For example, Ukraine’s 2004 winning entry, Ruslana’s “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=10XR67NQcAc">Wild Dances</a>,” opened with <a href="https://crees.ku.edu/trembita">the trembita</a>, a long alpine horn associated with the Hutsul people of the Carpathian Mountains. Armenia’s 2008 entry, Sirusho’s “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bridO-wD7c8">Qele, Qele</a>,” similarly combined a traditional Armenian <a href="https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/duduk-and-its-music-00092">duduk flute</a>, <a href="https://www.duduk.com/zurna-faq/">zurna trumpet</a> and <a href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/DYNYB_-O0n9/">dhol drums</a> with an upbeat dance track and contemporary pop vocals. While some scholars claim that these musical gestures strategically <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/book/68106">romanticize and exoticize regional cultures</a>, it’s a way to fuse national identity with modern music.</p>

<p>Other Eurovision Asia entrants also pulled from this playbook. Mongolia’s singer, Beck, <a href="https://www.clairethomasphotography.com/project/mongolian-fashion/">wore a deel</a>, the country’s traditional robe, <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sjZD9c4mxXk">while performing</a>. He also incorporated a traditional Mongolian string instrument into his performance.</p>

<p>Voting, which was open to the general public via an online form, began just before the first performance. Viewers were allotted eight free votes, on the condition that they <a href="https://www.eurovision.com/asia/how-to-vote/">had to vote for at least three different countries</a>. They could purchase 10 additional votes. The public accounted for half the votes, while a jury made up of representatives from each nation accounted for the other half.</p>

<p>Carmelle’s winning song – <a href="https://genius.com/Carmelle-sobra-sobra-lyrics">a Filipina women’s empowerment anthem</a> titled “Sobra-Sobra” (“Too Much”) – featured a repeated musical line played by <a href="https://centerforworldmusic.org/2021/09/instrument-kulintang/">a kulintang</a>, a Filipino percussion instrument, and a frenetic dance break. The song’s bridge <a href="https://asianstudies.cornell.edu/research/tagalog-filipino">was rapped in Tagalog</a>, the country’s national language.</p>

<p>As part of her reward, Carmelle will perform “Sobra-Sobra” at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Burgas, Bulgaria.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ccfIW1zsNdM?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The Philippines’ winning live performance at Eurovision Asia 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Europe, Asia … the world?</h2>

<p>No Eurovision competition would be complete without a measure of political controversy.</p>

<p>From <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cmr4y5dvlzneo">broadcaster boycotts over Israel’s participation</a> amid the war in Gaza to suspicions that <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2008/05/07/arts/07arts-FILMSAYSFRAN_BRF.html">Franco’s Spain rigged the 1968 Eurovision vote in its favor</a>, political disputes have long been part of the competition.</p>

<p>Normally, political statements are <a href="https://www.eurovision.com/newsroom/rules-of-the-contest/">not permitted in Eurovision</a>, though exceptions have been made for humanitarian causes. Ukraine’s <a href="https://theconversation.com/ukraines-eurovision-win-shows-us-that-despite-arguments-to-the-contrary-the-contest-has-always-been-political-182767">victory in Eurovision 2022</a> took place just a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the former Soviet republic. Oleh Psiuk, the frontman of Ukraine’s entrant, Kalush Orchestra, <a href="https://youtu.be/F1fl60ypdLs?si=MGxHfcTatP_OdLCF&amp;t=188">pleaded for support</a> for Ukraine at the end of the performance, which the European Broadcasting Union ended up allowing.</p>

<p>During Eurovision Song Contest Asia, Malaysia found itself at the center of controversy.</p>

<p>Malaysian entrant Aina Abdul, who wears a hijab in her public appearances, performed her song “Bluest Sky.” While Abdul was seen as a possible favorite, Malaysian audiences claimed that she ultimately did not score enough points <a href="https://manilastandard.net/showbiz/digital-media/314818693/eurovision-asia-voting-sparks-islamophobia-debate-after-malaysias-loss.html#:%7E:text=The%20online%20debate%20also%20raised,a%20role%20in%20the%20outcome">due to Islamophobia</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/wk6BMLVwGfY?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Malaysia’s live performance at Eurovision Asia 2026.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Another controversy arose due to the Malaysian broadcaster TV3’s coverage of the show. During the results segment at the end of the show, the camera feed of the Filipino spokesperson, the drag queen Vice Ganda, was cut from the Malaysian broadcast. <a href="https://www.malaymail.com/news/malaysia/2026/07/10/rtm-implements-strict-sop-to-filter-lgbt-content-across-tv-radio-and-digital-platforms-says-communications-ministry/227121">Malaysian broadcasting laws</a> restrict the airing of drag and LGBTQ+ content on television, radio and digital platforms.</p>

<p>In a comment to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2026/nov/16/eurovision-organisers-malaysia-removal-lgbt-footage-first-asian-contest">The Guardian</a>, Eurovision Director Martin Green said, “We are surprised and disappointed to learn that the broadcast of Eurovision Song Contest Asia was altered in Malaysia.”</p>

<p>“We take this matter seriously and will be writing to Voxovation,” Green added.</p>

<p>TV3 has yet to comment on the incident.</p>

<p>Here, there are also echoes of the European competition: Eurovision has embraced multicultural and pro-LGBTQ+ values to such an extent that <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2019/nov/27/hungary-pulls-out-of-eurovision-amid-rise-in-anti-lgbt-rhetoric">countries like Hungary</a> <a href="https://www.reuters.com/article/business/turkey-boycotts-eurovision-song-contest-over-lgbt-performers-idUSL5N1V06QB/">and Turkey</a> have withdrawn due to their governments’ incompatible sociopolitical values.</p>

<p>Eurovision Asia’s controversies prove that the European Broadcasting Union has a new – perhaps unexpected – set of geopolitical and sociopolitical values to navigate.</p>

<p>Television viewership for Eurovision Asia varied by market. In <a href="https://eurovoix.com/2026/11/15/vietnam-eurovision-asia-2026-reached-5-million-viewers/">Vietnam</a>, the show reached over 5 million viewers. The <a href="https://eurovoix.com/2026/11/17/thailand-400000-viewers-for-eurovision-asia-song-contest-2026/">host country’s broadcast</a>, however, only reached an average of 385,000 Thai viewers. These numbers pale in comparison to Eurovision 2026’s viewership of <a href="https://escxtra.com/2026/06/10/eurovision-song-contest-2026-attracts-131-million-viewers/">131 million viewers</a> across the 35 competing nations.</p>

<p>Nonetheless, <a href="https://www.standaard.be/media-en-cultuur/filipijnen-winnen-eerste-aziatische-songfestival-tweede-editie-zal-uitwijzen-of-er-een-toekomst-in-zit/164561147.html?utm_medium=referral&amp;utm_campaign=share">hype is already building</a> for the 2027 edition of Eurovision Asia. During a news conference in Bangkok, Voxovation executive <a href="https://eurovoix.com/2026/11/14/eurovision-asia-2027-discussions-to-commence-in-late-november/">Christer Björkman</a> confirmed that multiple cities have expressed interest in hosting, with China, Japan and Taiwan indicating that they’re open to participating in the future.</p>

<p>If more Asian broadcasters buy in, Eurovision will attract an even larger international audience, bringing Voxovation one step closer to turning the contest from a European tradition into a global phenomenon.</p>

<p>But time will tell whether Eurovision Asia can become something more than a European competition staged elsewhere.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291750/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

excerpt: Laos' contestant, Thinla, performs at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 in Bangkok on Nov. 14, 2026
body: Laos' contestant, Thinla, performs at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 in Bangkok on Nov. 14, 2026
Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP via Getty Images ABBA and Céline Dion came to the world’s attention thanks to the Eurovision Song Contest, an annual showcase of pop music, camp and spectacle
Filipino singer Carmelle is hoping that the Eurovision Song Contest Asia will serve as a similar springboard to international fame
On Nov. 14, 2026, Carmelle bested entries from 11 Asian countries to be crowned the Asian edition’s first-ever winner
The competition marked Eurovision’s boldest expansion of its format in its 70-year history
As a scholar of contemporary European popular music and politics , I study the ways in which Eurovision shapes notions of what it looks like and sounds like to be European

Knowing that the Asian edition would be organized by European broadcasting executives, I wanted to see how closely Eurovision Asia would resemble the flagship Eurovision, or whether it would carve out an identity of its own

Stops and starts Eurovision’s proposed expansion into Asia dates back to 2008, when the European Broadcasting Union – the transnational coalition of public service media organizations that has organized the Eurovision Song Contest since 1956 – announced plans for “ Our Sound – The Asia-Pacific Song Contest .” Originally slated to debut in 2010, the project never materialized

On March 31, 2026, however, Voxovation, a European-led production company that oversees the development of Eurovision’s spinoffs, announced that Bangkok would host the inaugural Asian competition in partnership with Thailand’s Channel 3 and S2O Productions
Eurovision Asia is now the second European Broadcasting Union-licensed global spinoff to make the airwaves
In 2022, Voxovation organized the American Song Contest , which included original songs by artists from all 50 U.S. states, five territories and Washington

Despite being promoted to the American public in a Super Bowl commercial featuring hosts Kelly Clarkson and Snoop Dogg, the competition failed to attract a large viewership and the spinoff wasn’t renewed. ‘You will be blown away!’ Given two decades of uncertainty, as well as the failure of Voxovation’s U.S. spinoff, some critics doubted whether the Asian version would succeed

And for a moment, it looked like everything might fall apart: In late October 2026, the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet reported that Eurovision Asia’s original budget of approximately US$4.5 million had been reduced by US$1 million
The European Broadcasting Union, however, confirmed that the show would go on as planned, and at 8:30 p.m

Bangkok time on Nov. 14, the show’s two hosts, Thai media personalities Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop, welcomed viewers from around the world tuning in via television broadcast and the YouTube livestream. “Maybe you’ve never heard of Eurovision before, or maybe you’re one of the hardcore Eurofans,” said Bishop. “It doesn’t matter, because you will be blown away by the talent here tonight!” For the next two-and-a-half hours, each country’s representative performed an original song, with Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên opening the show with her song “Em Tiên” (“Fairy Maiden”)
Vietnam’s entry had many of the spectacular ingredients of an ideal Eurovision entry: bilingual lyrics, large props, flashy outfits and a dance break
The song’s instrumentation included a flute accompanying Tiên’s melody and a bamboo xylophone
It concluded with a second, high-energy dance break reminiscent of electronic dance music genres
Vietnam’s live performance at Eurovision Asia 2026

The song’s use of traditional Asian musical signifiers followed the approach of the European entrants that have incorporated folk traditions to promote their national cultures to an international audience
For example, Ukraine’s 2004 winning entry, Ruslana’s “ Wild Dances ,” opened with the trembita , a long alpine horn associated with the Hutsul people of the Carpathian Mountains
Armenia’s 2008 entry, Sirusho’s “ Qele, Qele ,” similarly combined a traditional Armenian duduk flute , zurna trumpet and dhol drums with an upbeat dance track and contemporary pop vocals
While some scholars claim that these musical gestures strategically romanticize and exoticize regional cultures , it’s a way to fuse national identity with modern music
Other Eurovision Asia entrants also pulled from this playbook
Mongolia’s singer, Beck, wore a deel , the country’s traditional robe, while performing
He also incorporated a traditional Mongolian string instrument into his performance
Voting, which was open to the general public via an online form, began just before the first performance
Viewers were allotted eight free votes, on the condition that they had to vote for at least three different countries
The public accounted for half the votes, while a jury made up of representatives from each nation accounted for the other half

Carmelle’s winning song – a Filipina women’s empowerment anthem titled “Sobra-Sobra” (“Too Much”) – featured a repeated musical line played by a kulintang , a Filipino percussion instrument, and a frenetic dance break
The song’s bridge was rapped in Tagalog , the country’s national language
As part of her reward, Carmelle will perform “Sobra-Sobra” at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Burgas, Bulgaria
The Philippines’ winning live performance at Eurovision Asia 2026
Europe, Asia … the world? No Eurovision competition would be complete without a measure of political controversy

From broadcaster boycotts over Israel’s participation amid the war in Gaza to suspicions that Franco’s Spain rigged the 1968 Eurovision vote in its favor , political disputes have long been part of the competition
Normally, political statements are not permitted in Eurovision , though exceptions have been made for humanitarian causes
Ukraine’s victory in Eurovision 2022 took place just a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the former Soviet republic
Oleh Psiuk, the frontman of Ukraine’s entrant, Kalush Orchestra, pleaded for support for Ukraine at the end of the performance, which the European Broadcasting Union ended up allowing
During Eurovision Song Contest Asia, Malaysia found itself at the center of controversy

Malaysian entrant Aina Abdul, who wears a hijab in her public appearances, performed her song “Bluest Sky.” While Abdul was seen as a possible favorite, Malaysian audiences claimed that she ultimately did not score enough points due to Islamophobia
