title: The world’s most powerful frenemies talk nuclear weapons
excerpt: From left, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and President Donald Trump take part in a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China. | Ma
body: From left, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and President Donald Trump take part in a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China. | Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

President Donald Trump is on his way back from China after a four-day Asia trip that included taking in a surreal cover of “Y.M.C.A.,” heaping praise on a noted kleptocrat, and making earnest — if slightly cringe! — declarations of star-crossed presidential friendship .  But the highlight of the trip was surely Trump’s unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the first between those countries’ leaders.  The three men sat around a comically large and reflective roundtable to discuss issues like reforming the United Nations, increasing the world’s supply of petroleum, and reducing the risk of nuclear war, which they all thankfully agree would be a bad idea
A major nuclear treaty between the US and Russia lapsed nine months ago , and China has been a sticking point to negotiating a new one
In fact, all three countries are — in one realm or another — major obstacles to each other’s geopolitical ambitions.  Accordingly, no breakthroughs were reached during their hour-long chat
But they did agree to keep chatting…including about nuclear proliferation
Go a little deeper View Link I was surprised to learn that there’s currently no nuclear arms control treaty between Russia and the US
The two countries had agreed to mutual limits on their nuclear arsenals under a series of arms-control agreements dating back to the early 1970s

But when the latest one lapsed in February, nothing replaced it. (This despite Trump’s decades-long enthusiasm for nuclear disarmament.)  How, exactly, did we get here? To find out, I reached out to Rose Gottemoeller , the chief negotiator of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, or New START — that US-Russia nuclear deal that just recently expired
The original START was signed in 1991, just before the collapse of the Soviet Union

For the first time, the two countries agreed not just to stop growing their nuclear arsenals, but to actively reduce their strategic weapons.  New START slashed their stockpiles even further: to 700 missiles, 800 launchers, and 1,550 deployed warheads, Gottemoeller said. (When you consider that the world had roughly 70,000 nuclear warheads at the peak of the Cold War, it’s a pretty massive accomplishment.) But New START was negotiated during a brief, shining, Obama-era moment of optimism for nuclear arms control
Then Russia started getting grabby in Ukraine, and that optimism curdled.  The treaty was extended once, in 2021, about a year before Putin began a full-scale invasion
Since then, neither country has been in a particularly diplomatic mood
On the contrary, both Trump and Putin have at times signaled they might be a little nuke-curious.  The good news, of course, is that neither president ever acted on that curiosity
And in fact, the lapse of New START earlier this year hasn’t triggered a buildup. “So far Russia and the United States are sticking with the status quo limits,” Gottemoeller told Vox
The bad news is that either country could reverse course, and there are complications to negotiating firmer limits in the future

One of the biggies is China, which is rapidly building up its own nuclear stockpile — and thus disincentivizing Russia and the US from cutting theirs back further.  That’s the context for this morning’s trilateral, where Trump spoke explicitly about nuclear arms control before heading into the closed-door meeting

Gottemoeller, for her part, said she was “hopeful” the summit would “be a catalyst for new talks with the Russians [and] also nudge open the door to first talks with the Chinese.”  We’ll have to wait and see about all that

But the three leaders did release a vague post-summit statement that reaffirmed “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” That, crucially, is  a callback to a statement that US and Russian leaders released in 1985 after a summit that reinvigorated nuclear arms-control talks
One link for later ➨ Talk to more strangers
That occasionally awkward but ultimately life-affirming small talk helps you feel connected to other people
And according to University of Kansas researcher Jeffrey Hall, it boosts your entire community, too
By offering “dignity to another person…and by stretching yourself outside just the people you know well, you’re actually building a healthier environment for all of us,” Hall says

Before you go… Did you know… that almost 15 percent of adults suffer from tinnitus — a persistent, often ringing sound in their heads? It was once believed to be psychosomatic, but new research suggests it’s the result of a very specific type of hearing damage
Today’s trivia: Which popular therapy method was influenced by Buddhism? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the name of the US soccer player who scored the game-winning penalty kick at the 1999 Women’s World Cup
That would be Brandi Chastain, who famously — iconically! — fell to her knees and tore her jersey off in celebration.

title: The astonishing toll of America’s food stamp cuts
excerpt: A child helps load boxes at a California food bank in January 2026. | Paul Bersebach/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images As we head into Tha
body: A child helps load boxes at a California food bank in January 2026. | Paul Bersebach/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images As we head into Thanksgiving, a holiday dedicated to abundance and sharing, millions of Americans are struggling to afford groceries

Children, in particular, are at risk, their parents forced to choose between listening to their baby cry because they’re hungry or watch them shiver because they can’t pay for heating as the weather turns cold
Many of us have felt the costs of everyday life getting steeper, squeezing people at the gas pump and the grocery store
But some folks are facing not only inflation but the loss of government benefits: Federal assistance for food has been drying up since the Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last year

According to the estimates from the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, about 5.5 million people have fallen off of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (or SNAP) between the law’s passage in July 2025 and July 2026 — a 13 percent decline in just one year
About 2 million of the people who lost benefits are children
At this point, SNAP participation has reached a 17-year low, the lowest it’s been since the Great Recession, and not because people don’t need it
View Link It is as acute of an affordability crisis as any that Americans are facing right now

Nearly 1 in 4 US adults experienced food insecurity in 2025, according to the Urban Institute ; 8 percent said in a recent federal survey that their household often or sometimes did not have enough to eat

When people struggle to afford food, they get desperate: Parents start skipping meals so their kids can eat, they delay turning on their furnace when temperatures drop, they can’t afford gas or other basic household needs. “People are struggling, and we hear that and see that specifically in what is supposed to be an emergency food system, food pantries
They are reporting that they are seeing more people now than the pandemic

It’s not in a good place for families,” Gina Plata-Nino , director of SNAP policy and advocacy at the Food Research & Action Center, told me. “Every family is really feeling this — and what’s supposed to be a buffer when people hit a hard time is being taken away.” While Democrats spent more time on the campaign trail talking about the OBBBA’s Medicaid cuts, some of them also criticized the GOP for gutting food stamps
In announcing his bid to be House speaker, Rep
Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) said Democrats should restore SNAP’s funding during their first 100 days in power
A bipartisan deal has been percolating to delay some of the cuts and stem the bleeding
Congress says they want to address this burgeoning hunger crisis

How Trump and the GOP cut food assistance for millions When writing the OBBBA, Republicans wanted to prioritize cutting down on social services and alleged “fraud, waste, and abuse,” so they passed several measures meant to restrict SNAP eligibility and limit funding for the program
The law forced more adults to comply with the program’s onerous work requirements, raising the age of people expected to work from 55 to 64 for childless adults
More parents of younger children were also required to meet certain job-related standards in order for their families to continue getting assistance
The law also required states to contribute funding for the program for the first time if their enrollment “error” rates are too high, which has pushed states to require people to reapply for benefits

It also placed new restrictions on how the assistance money could be spent (rolling back previous allowances for utility and internet costs) and, in a sop to the GOP’s anti-immigration hardliners, the law cut eligibility for migrants who aren’t in the US permanently, even if they are here legally. “Democrats will scream ‘cuts,’ but what they’re really defending is a wasteful program that discourages work, mismanages billions, and traps people in dependency,” House Speaker Mike Johnson said in a statement last June

He put it even more bluntly in an interview with Face the Nation : “We have not cut SNAP.” Sign up for the Good Medicine newsletter Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems

How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy

And yet, millions of people have dropped from the program’s rolls since the OBBBA became law — again, including as many as 2 million children — and not because they were committing fraud or were too lazy to find work
In some states, the decrease has been very steep: Arizona saw its SNAP participation decline by roughly 50 percent in one year
Another nine states — Florida, Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Kansas, Nebraska, Nevada, Oklahoma, and Texas — have had their programs’ enrollment drop by more than 20 percent since last summer

Not all of this decline can be blamed on the Republican bill; even the left-leaning CBPP acknowledges that enrollment had already started to fall before Trump signed it as pandemic-era provisions expired and the economy improved.  But the rate of decrease has been accelerating in the year-plus since the OBBBA passed, as states crack down on enrollment in order to minimize their cost-sharing responsibilities under the law’s new rules
The legislation penalizes states for paying too much in benefits, and also paying too little, and also if there are any clerical errors in a person’s application

So, for those reasons, states have a strong incentive to simply force everyone to redo the paperwork — and we know from prior experience that more paperwork means more people who should be eligible losing their benefits. “I think that the thing that is contributing most to the acceleration in the declining enrollment are state-level policy changes related to the cost shift and getting their payment error rate under control,” Lauren Bauer , a fellow of economic studies at the Brookings Institution, told me

It has “prompted states to really tighten their belts and start making it much harder to get on the program, even for people who otherwise would be eligible in the absence of this policy change.” The new work requirements and other eligibility restrictions have also begun to take effect nationwide, and experts therefore expect the enrollment trends to get worse; Arizona, with its 50-percent decline in SNAP enrollment, could be a preview of what’s to come across the country.  “I do think that we are in the middle of this story… [This could be] the worst-case scenario of states learning from each other,” Bauer told me, “where Arizona starts telling everybody how they’re doing it and we see catastrophic declines in enrollment among people who otherwise should be eligible because everyone is so scared.” How bad it gets remains to be seen
But what’s clear at this point is that enrollment has not been shrinking because fewer Americans need this food assistance, as Diane Schanzenbach of Georgetown University wrote for Econofact

As CBPP’s analysts wrote in their own review of the data: “It’s very unlikely that reduced need is driving the decline in SNAP participation.” Instead, people are getting removed because they have trouble with the paperwork, or they may not even know they need to fill out new paperwork, or the state’s social services office may be inundated with a backlog of applications to check

As more people depend on the gig economy to make ends meet, they may be working unusual hours that make it more difficult to prove they meet the new requirements .  “What [the One Big Beautiful Bill Act] has done is that it has increased the time tax on families and the red tape,” Plata-Nino said

And because children only receive assistance through their parents — as opposed to getting it directly, like they do with survivor benefits after a parent dies — kids are particularly vulnerable to losing access because their parent has lost access

All this means that people are going into credit card debt just to pay for their basic household needs, or are simply going without. “We hear from families who don’t turn on the heat, who only take one bath a week, that only the baby gets warm water, and even in the winter, they’re getting cold water,” Plata-Nino said. “We hear from families who turn on the heating plates to warm up their house because they don’t have it

It really is incredibly challenging.” And if more people are struggling to afford food because they no longer receive government assistance, that is going to have consequences for their long-term health

One metaanalysis of the relationship between food insecurity and adverse health outcomes found that not having assured access to food was associated with 22 different negative health effects, including stress and depression, poor sleep, diabetes and hypertension, and anemia.  Kids experience a wide range of negative physical and mental health effects from hunger, which can impact their development for years

And while they have historically been able to rely on getting at least one good meal at school, declining SNAP enrollment also means fewer free school lunches through community eligibility, Bauer said. “People do turn to the charitable sector

But there is a reduction in the quantity and quality of food that you intake, and there are consequences to that,” Bauer said. “In terms of your health, both mental and physical, as well as other outcomes — especially for children, in terms of school attendance and school performance.” In other words, the situation for SNAP is dire as Democrats are coming into power

What now? What Congress could do to make food more affordable If there is any good news, it’s that Democrats’ enormous wins in the 2026 midterms are motivating lawmakers to do something about the looming SNAP cuts, potentially even before the new year

title: Come to GTA VI for the crime spree. Stay for the manatee.
excerpt: In Grand Theft Auto IV, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades. | Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive
body: In Grand Theft Auto IV, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades. | Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive There are plenty of reasons to be excited for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, which came out today
There are the heists, the incredibly realistic depictions of Florida , the surprisingly deep romance , and, you know, the car theft
It’s been 13 years since the last installment of the incredibly popular game series — basically an eternity in 2026 terms
But personally, I’m interested in the pelicans in flight at sunset and the green scales of an iguana in the street, as seen in the game’s second trailer
There are more than 170 animals in the game, like alligators, manatees, and frogs
There are also 62 species of birds, and players can pull out binoculars and record them all in a logbook
So this stuff is basically catnip for me, and I’m not the only one

There are Reddit threads full of excited birdwatchers who are saying that crime sprees will come second to birding in the new game, or that they want to get one of the game’s protagonists, Lucia, some cute birding outfits
The top comment in the New York Times’s review of the game says, “my roommate gets to play the actual game
I get to find all 67 [sic] species of birds

Truly a game for everyone.” features more than 170 species. | Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive" data-portal-copyright="Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive" /> While most of the game takes place in Vice City, which is developer Rockstar’s take on Miami, players start in a fictional version of the Florida Keys and can visit places like the Everglades and other national parks
In real life, this is one of the richest ecosystems in the country; Florida is home to more than 700 terrestrial animals , thousands of fish, and over 500 species of migratory and year-round birds

And with GTA VI, Rockstar is going even more immersive than it did in another one of its games, Red Dead Redemption 2, by adding features like bioluminescence, feather types, and accurately depicting how hair and fur are rendered for its wide variety of animals

View this post on Instagram “Florida has a diverse animal ecosystem that we wanted to faithfully include across all the different biomes in Leonida — urban and rural environs, aquatic life both inland and ocean, and the wetland habitats like the swamps and Everglades,” Rockstar’s vice president of dynamic art, Michael Kane, told Game Informer back in September (I reached out to Rockstar for comment but didn’t hear back by publication time)

I wouldn’t be surprised if some people spend way longer than strictly necessary wandering around in the opening areas, looking for one last bird to strike off their list.  Honestly, even though I’d call myself a gamer , I wasn’t entirely sure I’d play GTA VI
There’s just so much hype, and I was expecting it to mostly be another super-violent game about committing crimes
And of course that is part of it, but I love how it also seems to give people the option to take a moment and appreciate the natural world
To be fair, the game will also feature hunting of some of these animals, but I personally will be steering away from the Teddy Roosevelt school of conservation
It’s not the kind of thing you’d expect from a triple-A blockbuster, and maybe it’ll even get players to care more about biodiversity

Who knows, maybe afterward they’ll be motivated to, you know, touch grass. “We’ve been painting birds on the walls of caves and writing songs about them for millennia, and it makes total sense to me that this sort of wonder that we get from birds would find an expression in the very contemporary form of art that is a video game,” said Ethan Linck , an assistant professor in the Department of Ecology at Montana State University who stressed that he is not a gamer himself. “I could totally see someone who might not have any background in natural history or birdwatching get into this fun diversion in the game and then discover that they can basically do the exact same thing in real life using apps like eBird and iNaturalist
It’s no longer an old-person hobby.” Speaking of which, I have to go explore the Everglades myself

title: Do you feel like you can’t afford to have kids? This might be why.
excerpt: Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) speaks during a news conference on the Family and Medical Leave Act at the US Capitol on February 1, 2023. | Alex Wong/Getty Images Wh
body: Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) speaks during a news conference on the Family and Medical Leave Act at the US Capitol on February 1, 2023. | Alex Wong/Getty Images When it comes to wanting kids, the size of your paycheck seems to matter less than which way it’s moving

That’s one of the key findings in the 2026 American Family Survey, released Thursday by the Wheatley Institute at Brigham Young University and the Deseret News, which has been conducted annually since 2015

This year’s survey was conducted by YouGov among 3,000 Americans, along with an additional 1,500 adults ages 18 to 40.  Among childless adults under 50, 44 percent of those whose finances improved over the past year said they definitely want children, compared with 24 percent of those whose finances got worse

Income made much less of a difference: 29 percent of those earning under $50,000 said they definitely want kids, compared with 32 percent of those earning $100,000 or more. “Whether your finances are going up or down tells people more about the future than does your income now,” said Andrew Cherlin, a professor emeritus of sociology at Johns Hopkins University who studies family formation and wasn’t involved in the survey
View Link Young adults were also more likely than older Americans to say they need certain things in place before having a baby, like financial stability, an established career, or a house

Higher earners named even more conditions. “Income just doesn’t determine all of this,” said Jeremy Pope, a political scientist at BYU and one of the survey’s authors. “But I do think people care about security, they just define it differently depending on their situation.” Because parenthood is a long-term commitment, people “want to feel certain that the conditions they need to actually raise children for 18, 20, 25 years will be in place,” Karen Benjamin Guzzo, the director of the Carolina Population Center at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, told me

For decades, Americans have been told, by politicians, employers and the culture at large, that responsible people get their ducks in a row before having kids, or risk failing their children and going broke in the process
But it’s also an increasingly impossible standard to meet
Fewer people have stable jobs they can count on for years, and even people with W-2 employment and savings are less sure about what’s coming
And there’s no way to know for certain how having a kid will go
Still, policymakers who care about family formation should take note

Measures that give people a more lasting sense of security, like making homeownership more affordable , making child care assistance permanent or passing federal paid family leave , can do far more to help people feel ready to start a family than the kinds of policies Americans have watched come and go, like the one-year expansion of the child tax credit or pandemic-era stimulus checks .  In the short term, it’s also a warning sign that persistent inflation, tariffs, and the Iran war, which have combined to lower Americans’ real wages this year , may have downstream social effects

And looking ahead, relieving workers’ anxiety about their place in the AI era isn’t just a labor story — the more confident they feel about their future earnings, the more likely they might be to envision having children
Those who want kids may need to rethink what “ready” really looks like, but elected officials also need to do more to make people feel secure enough to try
A future that’s hard to picture The American Family Survey asked people whether their finances had gotten better, worse or stayed the same over the past year
Those whose finances had gotten worse were the least likely to say they definitely wanted kids, and those whose finances had improved were the most likely

Pope said the finding intrigued him and that more research is needed, but he has a theory. “I do think people think prospectively about this,” he told me. “I do think small changes make a difference to what you believe about the future.” For a lot of young adults, that future is hard to picture
About a third of childless adults under 40 who want kids told the survey researchers they couldn’t say when, or whether, they’d ever feel financially ready
And that share didn’t shrink as people got older
It stayed around 30 percent from their late 20s through their late 30s
Other recent research supports the idea that young people feel less sure about what’s coming
The Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia found this month that young adults’ sense of financial security and their outlook on the future have fallen more sharply than older adults’ since early 2025

And this fall’s Harvard Youth Poll found that , for the first time in its history, slightly more Americans ages 18 to 29 expect to be worse off financially than their parents than expect to be better off
The American Family Survey doesn’t prove that concerns about the future are keeping people from wanting kids

Melissa Kearney, an economist at the University of Notre Dame who studies birth rates, told me the findings “could also be showing that people who want kids are more likely to [be] on a positive financial trajectory, and people who don’t want kids are subject to more uncertainty or downside financial risk.”  Pope thinks that’s less likely but couldn’t rule it out

He also noted that the survey captures what people say they want, and people who express a general interest in having kids might not follow through. “It doesn’t mean you’re out there buying prenatal vitamins or something,” he said

More money, longer checklists The survey also gave people a list of eight things, such as financial stability, a career, a house, or marriage, and asked which ones they consider extremely important to have before a first child
Young adults identified more of them than older Americans did
Financial stability was at the top, chosen by 68 percent of adults under 40
They were also much more likely than people over 40 to say they needed an established career first (48 percent versus 32 percent) or a house (30 percent versus 20 percent)
Higher earners actually had longer checklists
Young adults earning $100,000 or more picked an average of 3.9 items they considered extremely important to have in place first, compared with 3.3 for those earning under $50,000
Cherlin, who has long written about marriage becoming a “capstone” of adult life rather than an early foundation, said the same thing has happened with kids

For wealthier young adults, he told me, having a child is “something you only do when the rest of your life is in order.” People with higher incomes don’t worry as much about providing kids the basics, Cherlin added, “but they are concerned about whether they can maintain their middle-class lifestyles.” Kearney offered a related explanation. “It’s all relative,” she said

High earners “might simply have an even higher bar for what they need to feel economically secure or sufficiently ‘ready’ to bring children into their lives.” Kearney’s own research adds another wrinkle

In a forthcoming paper, she and her co-authors found that never-married, childless adults in their late 20s and early 30s didn’t rate a hypothetical life with children any more favorably when it also came with ample finances or a home, but they did when it came with a fulfilling relationship

To her, it’s another sign that money isn’t the whole story. “While income and prices still matter, something beyond income and prices is driving the generational shift that we’re witnessing in the family formation decisions of young adults,” she said
What could help Money still matters, though, and many Americans are struggling

This year, 42 percent told the American Family Survey they’d faced a serious financial hardship in the past year, like going hungry, missing an important bill, or skipping medical care because of cost
That’s up from 35 percent last year, and the highest since the survey started asking in 2016

title: What does America get from the blue wave? It depends who wins this crucial argument.
excerpt: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) poses for a photo with newly elected Democratic senators in his office in the US Capitol Building on November 9, 202
body: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) poses for a photo with newly elected Democratic senators in his office in the US Capitol Building on November 9, 2026, in Washington, DC. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty When a party loses badly in an election cycle, what typically ensues is a frenzy of finger-pointing as different voices and factions advance their theory of what went wrong
In the wake of the 2026 blue tsunami, Democrats have a happier problem: They get to argue over who gets most credit for this smashing win

Indeed, prominent members of the two main sides in the party’s long-simmering civil war — progressives and moderates — barely paused to take a breath before arguing that the results precisely vindicated their theories of what American voters want, what makes for effective politics, and where the Democratic Party should go

Key takeaways Moderates point out that most Democrats who flipped key Senate states distanced themselves from progressives and the left on some issues, and argue that more solidly progressive candidates won by less impressive margins
Progressives point out that winning Democratic candidates, even in red states, embraced the rhetoric of economic populism, criticizing billionaires and corporations
Progressives argue that only major structural reforms to the economy can satisfy voters; moderates are urging a more limited focus on the cost of living
Democratic leaders will have to decide whose case is more persuasive as they shape the party’s governing agenda
The progressives say that winning candidates broadly ran on bold economic populist platforms , frequently criticizing billionaires and corporations
They point out that some very progressive or left candidates won in tough territory

And they say the results vindicate their preference for fiercely resisting the Trump administration rather than compromising with it.  “By and large, Democratic winners check two boxes,” Adam Green of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee told me. “One is fighting the status quo and being believed when they say they want to shake up a broken economic and political system
The second is challenging corporate power
That’s been a throughline everywhere.” The moderates, in contrast, argue that candidates who flipped key House and Senate seats are in key ways moderate
They say that the most progressive candidates in tough races tended to underperform the national trend

And they point out that, since 2024, Democrats across the party have recalibrated on issues like climate change, border security, crime, and identity issues, to get better in touch with voter concerns — a win for moderation, they say. “It’s pretty clear that the majorities we enjoy now were made by moderates,” Matt Bennett, co-founder of the center-left group Third Way, told me. “Just in terms of how these people ran in South Carolina and Mississippi and Alaska and Iowa — they did not run as full-throated progressives.” These arguments may sound a bit petty, and sometimes they are

But the stakes are actually quite high, because the lessons Democrats take from these midterms — the story they agree to tell themselves about why they won — will shape their choices about how to govern

If the moderates win the day, we can expect the next Democratic majorities — and perhaps the next presidential nominee — to have a cautious approach, carefully gauging the state of public opinion and trying not to get carried away by progressive advocacy or passions

But if the progressives make a convincing case that a bolder approach can spur sweeping electoral victories, they’ll be able to more effectively argue that the party should go big — in its clashes with the Trump administration, in legislation, in the 2028 presidential race, and in the next Democratic presidency
Did moderates do better than progressives? The first problem with adjudicating this debate: There’s no agreement on which candidate fits into which camp

Is Annie Andrews, Democrats’ victorious Senate candidate in South Carolina, a bold progressive because of her longtime gun control support, her history of spicy partisan commentary on social media, and her criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza? Or is Andrews a moderate because she supports a constitutional amendment requiring the US to have a balanced budget, she ran an ad saying she opposed “biological men playing in women’s sports,” she opposed Medicare for All , and she criticized the Democratic Socialists of America as “un-American and unhinged”? The reality is that Andrews, like several other Democratic candidates who flipped key Senate races, is a bit like the classic optical illusion that can look like either a rabbit or a duck, depending on where you focus.  They aren’t old-style moderates from central casting

But they did distance themselves from progressives and the left on certain topics — most often, in opposing Medicare-for-all , on trans issues involving children and sports, and in criticizing the Biden administration’s border security record (which, notably, even progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed did )

Liam Kerr, of the center-left group Welcome PAC, pointed to Josh Turek in Iowa and Adam Hamilton in Kansas. “Josh Turek said, ‘I’m a proud moderate and I’m running a radically centrist campaign.’ Adam Hamilton said he’s a self-described centrist against the extremes — the extremes, plural,” Kerr told me

There were, however, Senate candidates who much more ambiguously came out of the party’s left faction — such as El-Sayed in Michigan, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, Troy Jackson in Maine, and democratic socialist Angie Nixon in Florida

All but Nixon won their races.  But, electoral analysts like the New York Times’ Nate Cohn argue , all also “underperformed” the national trend. (El-Sayed, for instance, won Michigan by seven when Democrats won nationally by 14 points.) “Many of the weakest Democratic results — those where the party fared relatively poorly given the national environment and the characteristics of the state or district — came in races where Democrats picked progressive candidates in contested nominating fights this summer,” Cohn wrote
Still, other analysts, such as the leftist commentator Matt Bruenig, have pushed back , arguing that progressive underperformance was often small, inconsistent, or explained by more context

Nixon, for instance, lost her Senate race in Florida by 2.9 points, while the more mainstream Democratic nominee David Jolly, a former Republican Congress member, lost the governor’s race by 1.3 points

Is everyone an economic populist now?  The most common pushback from progressives to the “moderates did better” argument is to argue that the supposed moderates in fact ran as quite progressive when it comes to economic issues — and that they made criticism of billionaires and corrupt corporate interests central to their message. “Democrats won by being populist economic fighters who were unafraid to call out the corrupt politicians and corporate interests who have rigged the system at the expense of everyone else,” Sen
Elizabeth Warren wrote in an op-ed two days after the midterms

Warren cited many examples of victorious candidates in key red state races rhetorically calling out billionaires and corporations, advocating for economic power, criticizing a rigged system, and calling for policies like blocking grocery store mergers and breaking up healthcare monopolies

Elizabeth Warren, told me: “Whether it was in South Carolina or Iowa or Kansas, candidates were saying a pretty comparable message to what we were saying in Maine and Michigan — or even in very blue states — about what my old boss would call a rigged system.” The relative moderates I interviewed tended to agree that a shift had occurred, though some had different interpretations of what it meant
Adam Jentleson, a former Democratic Senate aide and founder of the center-left Searchlight Institute, largely endorsed the shift

He told me Democrats have always been strongest when they “lean hard into economic populism, but have some flexibility on other issues,” an approach his group describes as “heterodoxy.”  Third Way’s Bennett tried to draw a distinction between what he called Bernie Sanders’s “shotgun populism” — which he characterized as “rich people are the problem, all of them are bad” — versus Georgia Sen

Jon Ossoff’s “rifle shot approach,” in which “specific people and organizations are the problem, not everybody who is wealthy.” (Bennett prefers the latter.) Yet Green, of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, argued to me that the moderates were now belatedly embracing economic populism because progressives won the argument. “The people who Third Way calls ‘moderate’ basically ran on the [Zohran] Mamdani message of tying billionaire power and corruption to people’s higher prices,” Green said. “If they want to call that moderate, great! That means we won the battle of ideas.” Complicating things is that Democrats have long incorporated some of the themes from this year’s midterms: Every modern Democratic president, from Bill Clinton to Barack Obama to Joe Biden, ran on taxing the rich, expanding benefits, and standing up for the little guy in some fashion, even as their policy agenda and tone differed from each other and from politicians like Sanders.   Do the voters want a laser focus on lower prices — or do they want more ambitious progressive reforms to reshape the economy? But even if there’s general agreement that many candidates won on a message of “affordability” or even economic populism, there’s much more disagreement on how to translate that into policies that will deliver voters what they want
Several progressives I interviewed argued that voter concern about affordability should not be misread as an exclusive focus on gas and grocery prices

Voters who rejected the status quo want to crack down on corporate influence writ large, build a more expansive safety net, and make deep changes to how power is distributed, they said. “Everybody wants to call this the affordability moment, the cost of living crisis
Yes, people have been experiencing — having a hard time making ends meet, rent, groceries, etcetera

But I truly believe it is more than that,” Elizabeth Wilkins, president of Roosevelt Forward, the advocacy affiliate of the progressive think tank the Roosevelt Institute, told me. “People are experiencing a deep sense of precarity and anxiety about their economic future.” Wilkins said that Democrats should be wary of “ incrementalist approaches ” that fail to “restructure power for the long haul.” The next Democratic agenda, she said, should try to “demonstrate to people that we are willing to take on the existing power structure.” Ramamurti pointed me to an article he wrote warning of the “ affordability mirage ,” and said the public’s concerns were deeper. “These concerns, in my mind, are not just purely about affordability,” he said. “They are structural concerns about how the economy is set up, and about the unresponsiveness of our political institutions to the concerns of the public.”  Both Wilkins and Ramamurti pointed to sectoral bargaining — that is, letting workers across entire industries collectively bargain together, rather than separately in each company — as an example of a major reform that could alter the balance of power between workers and employers.  Yet moderates and those on the center-left argue that the party should take the polls in which voters consistently complain about the cost of living quite literally. “The American people do not want to pay for your political project,” Jerusalem Demsas, founder of the liberal publication The Argument (and a former Vox colleague), wrote Wednesday. “The 2024 and 2026 electorates spoke as clearly as possible: They are mad about the price of consumer goods and services.” Per this line of thinking, Democrats should not attempt to claim a mandate to tear down the existing economic system, but should rather focus on trying to actually address voters’ cost concerns — for instance, by passing the permitting reform bill that congressional Democrats are currently divided over, since that could help bring down energy prices
For now, just as candidates often sang from the same hymnal on the trail, there’s more overlap between left and center than you might expect

Speaker-in-waiting Hakeem Jeffries has backed a healthcare agenda, for example, that would both reverse Trump’s Medicaid and Affordable Care Act cuts and implement a Sanders-backed plan to lower the Medicare age to 55 and add new benefits like dental care
But that unity may be harder to maintain over time, especially if Democrats acquire the presidency after 2028 and their bills have a greater chance of becoming law

That’s partly because, as some moderates emphasize, progressives’ dreams of big new spending programs are going to crash headlong into the country’s huge deficit problem — which, they say, is connected to the cost-of-living problem, since it’s associated with higher interest rates on home mortgages and car loans

title: How Nvidia’s chaos trickles down to you
excerpt: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sits for an interview with Bloomberg News in London on October 14, 2026. | Bloomberg via Getty Images If you didn’t know a lot ab
body: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sits for an interview with Bloomberg News in London on October 14, 2026. | Bloomberg via Getty Images If you didn’t know a lot about Nvidia a month ago, what you know now is salacious, essential, and probably a little bit misleading.  The multitrillion-dollar chipmaker has primarily been in the news because its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang had a few affairs — one with a possible spy — and resigned

This has been a huge story, not just because of the sex scandal but also because Nvidia has been propping up the entire AI industry, as its primary chip supplier and frequent financier, and, by proxy, propping up the global economy
The downside risk is almost catastrophic: If Huang brings Nvidia down with him, the whole economic house of cards could collapse
Nvidia just reported its third-quarter earnings and beat estimates , seemingly setting up interim CEO Colette Kress for success (even if it ultimately disappointed Wall Street )
The company’s board also declared that it would not reinstate Huang , despite Huang’s very public willingness to be reinstated
So the company isn’t exactly in crisis mode
That doesn’t mean it will avoid a reckoning, But the reckoning is much broader than the Huang storyline — and if it comes, might even be beneficial

Nvidia is facing a raft of investigations and potential new regulations as a more AI-skeptical Congress prepares to take power , not to mention growing competition from tech giants, like Google , that have started making their own highly advanced chips for AI
There are also signs that the chips that made Nvidia so profitable won’t be as critical in the next chapter of the AI era
So maybe Nvidia was already in trouble before the world learned more than it wanted to about Jensen Huang’s sex life
More broadly, a shakeup in the apparently very precarious AI industry could end up being a good thing
Free market capitalism tends to thrive when there’s more competition
And, just maybe, we stand to benefit from more scrutiny into tech giants like Nvidia and their executives

There’s reason to believe real shakeup at Nvidia — even a fall from its exalted perch and its role as the money factory of the AI world — could turn out to be the right thing for consumers, healthy for the market, and useful in the event of the AI bubble bursting
Why Nvidia matters to normies (yes, even you) You might be wondering what any of this has to do with you
Nvidia’s top chips can cost more than a car , and precious few humans have ever even seen one
Why should the escapades of a leather jacket-loving tech executive distract you from your hobbies or affect your daily life? For the most part, it won’t
Even if you’re an enthusiastic Claude or ChatGPT user, what happens to Nvidia won’t change the way you use this technology
AI as we know it won’t immediately get better or cheaper if competition heats up in Silicon Valley
The stock market might get shakier, though

In that sense, we’re all in this together. “American consumers likely may not feel Nvidia’s pain in their own pocketbook, but they may likely feel it in their 401(k),” said Margaret O’Mara , a historian at the University of Washington. “We’re all stockholders, whether we like it or not.” If you’re enrolled in your employer’s 401(k), you probably own some Nvidia stock, either directly or through a mutual fund
Even if you don’t, any company as rich and central as Nvidia can cause real shock waves in the economy
The simple explanation for this is that Nvidia and a tiny handful of big tech company stocks make up a massive share of the stock market
The “Magnificent Seven” stocks account for about a third of the entire S&P 500 index — yes, that’s seven out of 500 total companies — and they haven’t been doing all that well lately

At its peak in May, Nvidia alone accounted for nearly 9 percent of the S&P 500. (It’s currently around 6 percent.) That meant that when its stock tanked following the Huang scandal, it knocked thousands of dollars off millions of retirement accounts
This is not a reason to rebalance your portfolio, and I’m not in the business of giving investment advice
But the panic people might be feeling right now around the future of Nvidia and the possibility of an AI bubble is a helpful reminder that panicking is almost always a bad idea
An instructive example is the Panic of 1873 , when one dominant company faltered, caused a run on the banks, and pushed the United States into what’s now called the first Great Depression
Plus, because the company is just so big, it’s actually pretty hard to get Nvidia stock out of your retirement accounts completely
The good news, on this front, is that Nvidia probably isn’t going anywhere

We learned on Tuesday evening that the company continues to make money hand over fist , with $115 billion in revenue in the third quarter of this year, which is up over 100 percent from the same time last year

The advanced graphics chips, or GPUs, that Nvidia makes continue to be the gold standard for AI tasks, and perhaps more importantly, Nvidia has built an impressive moat around its chip business to shield itself from competitors
Nevertheless, the competitors have been moving in
AI has gotten so good at writing software, for instance, that it’s possible to rewrite code designed for Nvidia chips to run on those made by competitors like AMD

Google is also making advanced chips called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) as a challenger to Nvidia’s GPUs. (Google actually rolled out a whole new generation of TPUs in early November, just a few days before Jensen Huang resigned.) Amazon has been filling AWS data centers and powering Anthropic’s Claude with its Trainium chips , another competitor to Nvidia GPUs
Microsoft, meanwhile, has its Azure Maia chips and expects higher demand after this Nvidia drama.  A lot of companies still want to buy Nvidia products, though

Nvidia has been able to pull in 75 percent or more in profits on its chip sales because they’re in such high demand, according to Chris Miller , a professor of international history at Tufts and the author of Chip Wars: The Fight for the World’s Most Critical Technology . “Nvidia’s argument has always been, ‘Yeah, we charge a pretty thick profit margin on top of our chips, but we give you the best possible outcome,’” Miller said. “But its pricing power would decline if the competition increases.” Competition, as any student of capitalism knows, should lead not only to lower prices but also more innovation and better-quality products
It’s still not clear what the downstream effects of cheaper, faster, more powerful AI chips might be, though
Most people encounter AI not through any direct contact with Nvidia, which sells its products to other companies
They use ChatGPT or Claude, and they may even pay a subscription fee for access to better models

title: The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles

This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth
Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell

Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents
But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases
Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver

How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us? —Amit Katwala Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration

But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure

title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
excerpt: Giving computers a nose: AI startup Osmo claims its model has reached "human-level olfactory intelligence" — roughly as capable as the average person at detecti
body: Giving computers a nose: AI startup Osmo claims its model has reached "human-level olfactory intelligence" — roughly as capable as the average person at detecting smells
The data problem: Fewer than 200,000 human smell descriptions existed before Osmo
The company built its own dataset of over 10 million labels, using teams of trained sniffers and spectrometers running around the clock
Real-world applications — and real skeptics: Osmo has worked with P&G on fragrances, identified insect repellents stronger than DEET, and helped spot counterfeit sneakers
But critics argue its big claims are undocumented and still heavily reliant on human judgment
Context is everything: Scientists warn the AI may miss what makes human smell uniquely powerful — the same molecule in Camembert cheese also appears in used diapers, yet we never confuse the two

Cracking that complexity could unlock medical diagnostics, the technology's biggest potential prize. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148816" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth

Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell

The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language
And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint
You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life

You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them
It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents
Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies

Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.  Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens
The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data
Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count

Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.  OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors
Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs
A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary
Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels

In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers
It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt
Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked
He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men
The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them

If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.  Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble

The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET
Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes
But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims

Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows , has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack , arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March
In response, Wiltschko says that “human perception isn’t a workaround for AI”. “Language models learn from what people have written
Smell is ultimately a human experience, so the model has to learn from humans to bridge chemistry and perception

That’s what lets it predict how people will experience a scent as well as the human nose does.” Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement

With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.  But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex
The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies
You don’t confuse the two because of the context.” In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much
But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models
Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies
For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says

body: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country
